Magneto-mechanical systems in cavity opto-mechanics utilize two-dimensional (2D) materials like graphene and transition metal dichalcogenides to detect tiny mechanical movements through modified cavity losses. Building on this, this study demonstrates that 2D materials can also serve as active transducers in cavity magnomechancial setups, facilitating precise quantum-state optimization of magnons within ferrite materials. Our findings employ stochastic variable-floquet magnomechanical cavity (FMMC) models, which integrate linearly broken-time-reversal symmetry caused by Stochastic telegraph processes governing permeation with 2D materials. We reveal that this configuration enables quantum-coherent control of magnons even in noisy environments. Specifically, graphene suspended in an external field allows for magnon cooling near the single-quantum limit, while Yttrium nitride cavities interacting with MoS<sub>2</sub> reach a novel quantum state near absolute zero temperature. These results open a new avenue for quantum engineering in magneto-mechanical domains.

Hot winds are thought to be a significant component of black hole feedback; however, their generation mechanisms and impact dynamics remain unclear. This study examines the properties and evolutionary tracks of these winds originating from low-luminosity active galactic nuclei (LLAGNs). We developed a analytical framework based on magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) to model this ejection, defining wind energy feedback efficiency as the ratio of wind energy injection to black hole accretion energy. Subsequently, we simulated 5000 galaxy evolution scenarios incorporating these winds and evaluated their evolution against X-ray observations of clusters and groups. Our results indicate that magnetohydrodynamical wind evolution is governed by group and cluster mass thresholds. In clusters, wind efficiency and evolution paths show considerable scatter. By fitting simulated galaxy evolution models to X-ray luminosity data from groups, we found a wide range of cluster X-ray luminosity evolution depending on wind efficiency, which must be accounted for when studying cluster evolution. Furthermore, we demonstrate that wind efficiency is uniquely determined by matching simulated heating to observed group X-ray luminosity trends. Finally, our findings show that wind evolution tracks are consistent with X-ray observations only if wind efficiency is less than 10%, which supports low efficiency magnetohydrodynamical wind models over jet-driven alternatives.

Theory demonstrates that policies structured with this integration achieve a lower theoretical upper bound on regret summing over $N$ time steps compared to those governed by traditional exploration strategies. Empirical evaluations confirm that inline optimization via Regret Minimisation successfully stabilizes learning dynamics in offline scenarios, whereas our proposed approach demonstrates superior transient learning performance through online trials.

Notably, nematic orientation displays robust spatial ordering, and the fluctuation-dissipation relation holds accurately for both nematic stresses and director fluctuations. The widespread adoption of transfer learning has driven advancements across diverse application domains. Programming languages, characterized by intricate syntactic rules and semantics along with varying degrees of abstraction, present unique challenges for generalizing knowledge from pre-trained models to practical applications. Existing research primarily focuses on pre-training language models to capture programming language features, subsequently fine-tuning them for specific tasks. However, this standard pipeline often fails to fully leverage rich pre-existing knowledge because: (1) fine-tuning diverse tasks may introduce conflicting pre-tuned skills, or conflicting information within each task may obscure useful signals; and (2) each downstream model retains only partial knowledge, resulting in suboptimal knowledge density across final systems. To address this, we introduce Knowledge Merging Ensemble Pre-training (KMEP), a framework designed to aggregate pre-trained knowledge efficiently for diverse tasks. KMEP operates in two phases. Firstly, using in-house compiled code corpora, it pre-trains foundational models via masked autoencoding. Secondly, it merges the resulting representations using a carefully selected loss function. This approach enables diverse models to retain comprehensive programming knowledge while interverting representations through better semantic alignment. Empirical evaluations across six downstream applications demonstrate that KEMeP significantly surpasses existing baselines. Specifically, it yields substantial gains—up to 3.3% macro F1-score—over ensemble ensemble pre-training approaches.

Wide-field photometry offers a robust method for calculating vertical aerosol optical depth while avoiding the need for absolute calibration. By monitoring the luminance of an unlit sky region across various elevations, the technique circumvents standard instrumental constraints. The study presents results from continuous observations of a sky region above Arecibo, Puerto Rico, spanning elevations from 30 to 85 degrees over a period of roughly 40 days during which stable cloud cover was absent. Observations were collected every 10 minutes using a 1.3-meter diameter telescope equipped with an 18-degree field of view, yielding a data set of 1,300 measurements covering two weeks in December 2020. The analysis reveals that, for elevations exceeding 30 degrees, the derived optical depth values remain consistent regardless of elevation, a finding supported by comparisons with data from similar wide-field studies. Additionally, the research demonstrates that instrumental scattering, which was not previously quantified, contributes between 10% and 30% to the total measured sky brightness above 30 degrees. The calculated optical depths align well with measurements from established radiometric sources, including A-Train satellites and ground-based total radiance sensors. A new validation approach was devised to confirm the reliability of the wide-field photometry outcomes.

Recent advancements in Neural Architecture Search (NAS) have yielded numerous high-performing models; however, significant progress toward comprehending the fundamental properties underlying optimal architectures remains elusive. In this study, we investigate the relationship between GENDO architecture properties and their performance by training a substantial cohort of candidate solutions. Our analysis reveals several key findings: (1) the macro structure exerts a dominant influence on architecture performance, yet NAS methods frequently optimize for micro-level details while overlooking macro-level flaws, creating many suboptimal variants; (2) for a given macro structure, performance varies widely across different configurations, suggesting that current search methodologies must accommodate this diversity; (3) an architecture's training dynamics serve as reliable indicators of its final accuracy, enabling the prediction of performance for architectures that remain untrained. Leveraging these observations, we propose GENDArch—a streamlined NAS framework utilizing a novel scoring mechanism grounded in training dynamics. Experimental results demonstrate that GENDArch efficiently identifies high-accuracy models, significantly trailing the efficiency of state-of-the-art methods.

This study presents an entirely new multiple access signal design within millimeter-wave multicasting environments. We introduce "Multi-Scale Waveform Construction" (MSWC), a framework capable of simultaneously enhancing the degrees of freedom for multicasting, achieving radio frequency-to-baseband waveform compression, and ensuring orthogonality at the receiver to mitigate inter-user interference. We demonstrate that MSWC achieves perfect multiple access spectral efficiency by establishing an exact equivalence between ms-waveforms and multi-channel convolutional neural networks. Furthermore, we formulate beamforming and pilot assignment as a joint optimization problem aimed at maximizing downlink sum-rate, while developing a decentralized, single-timeslot learning approach based on the MSWC framework to enable a globally optimal and near-optimal solution. Finally, we establish a robust connection between MSWC and modern model-based convoluted neural networks, thereby ensuring robustness in our optimization strategy. Extensive simulations confirm that the proposed approach attains a maximum system energy efficiency gain of 100% compared to existing methods employing multiple antennas at the receiver, alongside a data rate improvement of 80%. These results highlight MSWC's exceptional capability in enhancing spectral and energy efficiency.

An optimization task involves an agent seeking to maximize a utility function $u$ unknown to it, by querying an expert who provides the pairwise performance results of result pairs. Researchers have previously established that this learning process must occur online to be effective, based on the premise that querying the expert for preferences requires presenting pairs that appear comparable. This paper argues instead that an optimal utility function *can* be extracted from the preferences. We demonstrate that this function can be learned in both online and offline settings from those offline data. In our model, we describe each learned utility function as a linear combination of $m$ basis functions to encode the expert's domain knowledge. We propose an $m$-dimensional query method that projects the query space into an $m$-dimensional representation using an $m \times m$ orthogonal matrix. We show that using queries of size $m$, one can learn a function that approximates the true utility function within error. We further prove that an orthogonal query method with complexity $m$ yields an optimal utility function with approximation within error. We demonstrate that this approach scales to datasets with over 100,000 items and basis functions. We conclude that this technique is highly effective at: (1) scaling to very large datasets, (2) working with many basis functions, and thus encoding expert knowledge, and (3) being applicable to both offline and online learning scenarios.

This paper investigates privacy-preserving and robust aggregation techniques tailored for edge collaborative learning, specifically addressing non-IID data distributions and heterogeneous communication capacities. We introduce Weighted Power-P (WPM) aggregation, an enhanced method involving a learning component, which adapts traditional linear averaging by applying both sample- and client-level weights along with signed updates. Unlike linear approaches, WPM actively rebalances contributions based on the dispersion of local gradients, optimizing overall model performance. Consequently, we develop a cryptographic protocol enabling secure WPM aggregations, ensuring privacy guarantees for individual clients. Furthermore, we demonstrate through extensive experiments on non-IID datasets and networks with varying node communication abilities that our protocol successfully ensures secure privacy protection and improves robustness.

By analyzing over 1.5 million physics articles published between 1960 and 2006 on CiteSeerX, a vast citation database containing more than 100 million records, we address a significant limitation in previous literature: a reliance on small samples drawn from individual universities or disciplines. Our findings confirm that papers prepublished via arXiv attract more citations at similar age intervals. Furthermore, papers that were first submitted to arXiv prior to acceptance yield higher cumulative citations than those without a preprint. This advantage is particularly pronounced for works with longer half-lives, suggesting that prepublication enhances relevance and utility over time. Our analysis leverages a dataset of unprecedented scale, enabling robust statistical comparisons that advance understanding of digital scholarship metrics.

This paper introduces the "DaDoc" system, an application designed to convert raw instrument readings into structured laboratory documentation through seamless integration with laboratory equipment via laboratory information management software. DaDoc addresses prevalent challenges such as document backlogs and manual errors by automating data management processes. Specifically updating previous work presented at IUCC 2019, this revised manuscript includes additional empirical validation drawn from our collaborations within the European Muon Instrumentation Centre's first and second collaborations. User feedback indicates that DaDoc significantly cuts implementation times and effectively minimizes human mistakes while documenting results.

Recently, machine learning has proven highly effective in predicting material phase formations and mechanical properties, leveraging both experimental data and first-principles calculations. However, reliable prediction of kinetic processes—essential for understanding how materials form and transform—remains a significant challenge. Kinetic analysis often demands very large datasets to overcome the low probability events characteristic of problems like diffusion rates. To address this, we present a generative adversarial network strategy designed to enlarge training sets by synthesizing new data points from existing ones. We validate this approach through case studies on Al and Ti alloys, utilizing molecular dynamics simulations to analyze various thermal treatments. Ultimately, we demonstrate the efficacy of GAN-enhanced training sets in driving both phase prediction and material property assessment for materials science.

Subspace learning seeks to isolate graph nodes belonging to distinct groups, a task frequently employed in visual classification and clustering. Graph neural networks (GNNs) offer potential advantages over established subspace learning techniques by simultaneously performing dimensionality reduction and embedding. Yet, key inquiries remain unresolved: do GNNs truly uncover intrinsic dimensionality, and can they separate visual instances based on distinct subgroup labels? To address these issues, this paper introduces learning with graphs neural networks pre-assignment separation, a method designed to identify graphs with conditionally distinct node labels based on continuous representations. Our analysis demonstrates that GNNs effectively isolate distinct group labels and reduces nodes to their inherent intrinsic dimensions through the lens of inductive representation learning.

This study investigates the Universal Sampling (UFS) algorithm—a technique for efficiently generating binary matrices that mimic uniform randomness. Originally proposed by Cayton and colleagues in 2019 as a method for rapidly approximating K-means clustering on binary data, U-s was found to yield results nearly indistinguishable from those using uniformly random binary matrices. Though seemingly limited to uniform cases, we demonstrate that U-s can be extended to generate approximations for matrices drawn from arbitrary probability distributions. Our theoretical findings show that when applied to these broader scenarios, U-s still successfully produces binary matrices close to uniform while preserving the structural properties of the source matrix. Furthermore, we prove that these generated matrices retain key characteristics from the original uniform-like matrices. We also examine how K-means behaves when applied to binary matrices with general distributions. Under a diversity-based K-means setup, we prove that both matrices generated by U-s and directly generated uniform-like matrices yield clusterings from which the true columns of an underlying column-sparse matrix can be exactly recovered. Beyond theory, we conduct empirical tests showing that K-means clusters produced by U-s on binary data effectively identify and approximate the underlying column-sparse structure, even when using data generated from other distribution schemes.

Quantifying the uncertainties associated with Parton Distribution Functions (PDFs) is vital for precision predictions in high-energy collider physics. Standard methodologies typically calculate uncertainty bands by performing separate fits to experimental data at varying DGLAP evolution scales, followed by a statistical comparison of these distributions. An alternative approach updates PDFs iteratively via Bayesian inference alongside data at a fixed scale; however, this requires defining and fixing prior distributions for PDFs prior to the fit. This study introduces a fully Bayesian framework utilizing hybrid variational autoencoders to perform joint evolution and fitting of PDFs. By employing this method on the NNFit dataset, we demonstrate its efficacy. These results allow us: (i) validate that single-scale DGLAP evolution of prior distributions prior to fitting yields quantitatively similar uncertainty assessments compared to multi-scale fits; and (ii) identify key data-driven features within the Bayesian framework that affect PDF parameterizations.

ELKI functions as both an extensive testing suite and a versatile framework for performance evaluation~in~data mining. This tool supports statistical analysis, providing metrics such~as~mean, median, and standard deviation, alongside graphical outputs like line charts and heatmaps. While ELKI's capacity for high-throughput processing enhances its computational power, this capacity consumes substantial memory. To alleviate this memory burden, we developed an optimization technique that improves both scalability and efficiency. Furthermore, to facilitate a comprehensive performance comparison, we have established a web portal accessible at `elki.elki.info/performance/`.

We introduce a novel technique for generating large microcombs using sideband pumping on resonators that support only TEM$_{00}$ modes. By leveraging spacings between pump-sidebands lower than the microcavity mode density, this approach produces a spectrum with red-sidebands spaced according to the microcavity resonance frequencies. Spectral tilts are achieved simply by adjusting the relative phases among these side-pump components, enabling the compact control of multiple tiled microcombs for applications in integrated photonic systems.

We examine the training dynamics of quasi neural networks employing fixed weights on select layers, utilizing eigenvalues of the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) spanning multiple scales. By investigating operator splitting, we demonstrate that if the NTK's principal eigenvalue decays exponentially—measured against a specific eigenfunction corresponding to slower decay rates of higher-order components—the network's behavior mirrors that of an ideal neural network and degrades similarly to non-quasi architectures regarding those slower rates. Furthermore, our findings indicate that a network employing Heaviside activation functions fails to exhibit this decay, serving as a counterexample. In contrast, networks using smooth activations exhibit decay, while those with non-differentiable activations, such as ReLU, may show decay or fail to do so contingent upon network width and depth.

This study explores implications deriving from the proposed duality linking bulk gravitational systems to quantum error correction architectures, specifically focusing on how mutual information requirements in the interior translate to constraints on boundary entropies. While bulk entropies monogamy imposes mutual information restrictions that are universally satisfied by error correction codes, we demonstrate that this condition restricts specific classes of codes rather than merely designing monogamy-respecting structures. Notably, valid codes capable of yielding smooth geometric connections in regions outside the signaling causal wedge but inside the strong causal wedge satisfy these boundaries. Furthermore, we identify a family of codes where the resulting geometric configuration is fully determined by the boundary von Neumann entropies.

We examine the axioms defining a class of solutions to the solvable lattice model equation and demonstrate that their local state probabilities correspond to the branching rule of a corresponding quantum group, which we detail hereafter.

This work examines merging distinct stabilization methods within overdetermined systems of equations to create new signal recovery algorithms. We apply this approach to develop stabilization techniques applicable to equations exhibiting symmetry under group conjugation. Additionally, we demonstrate that integrating this scheme with an analogous method from previous research yields significant improvements in exact signal recovery. However, we also identify specific instability issues in stabilized algorithms when dealing with symmetry-related equations and propose further stabilization measures to mitigate these issues. All proposed methods and their corresponding properties are validated through extensive numerical simulations.

Coadding images serves as a basic image processing technique for creating extensive image catalogs, yet most current coaddition algorithms are proprietary and poorly documented. These methods frequently introduce unwanted artifacts, such as atypical and inconsistent PSF profiles for stars and non-physical image-scale variations. This study evaluates several coaddition strategies and proposes mathematical proofs to demonstrate that nonlinear approaches, including clipped-mean and the median, introduce a PSF that broadens excessively under sampling noise. In contrast, we show that linear coaddition methods, like DDT and convolution, preserve a consistent PSF profile and correctly summation the flux. Consequently, we advocate for the adoption of linear algorithms and provide the necessary Python code and libraries for the DDAA (Difference-Domain Deconvolution Addition) add process in the public domain for use by researchers and analysts.

Quantum verification is vital for certifying computational results from potentially unreliable quantum processors. While current protocols—typically involving fully interactive procedures—allow classically controlled validators to confirm quantum computation correctness, they struggle with computational efficiency. To address this, we introduce the first non-interactive quantum verification (CVQC) framework capable of confirming results from circuit models containing both unitary operations and quantum checks. Notably, our CVQC model addresses a limitation in prior non-interactive approaches which required validators to interact classically; instead, our protocol is practical for validators with limited quantum capabilities. Crucially, demonstrating that efficiently checking a polynomial number of computations is feasible, our protocol achieves this, addressing an issue where previous methods demanded extensive computations for polynomially many interactions.

Cellular morphology serves as a critical indicator in diagnostics and drug discovery, yet quantifying these features demands extensive, expert-labeled data—a resource often unavailable for many conditions. While data augmentation techniques typically enhance biomedical image analysis by mimicking variations in imaging parameters and capture angles, this work introduces an innovative approach using deep generative models for cell shape synthesis. This method specifically targets domain extensions pertinent to cell tracking and segmentation, including shape topology and background context, thereby addressing shape labeling scarcity. By evaluating the technique on both real and synthetic datasets using a standard 3D cell tracker, we demonstrate that the proposed method achieves performance comparable to current advanced data augmentation strategies.

Building upon established connections between circuit depth and feature persistence in reinforcement learning (RL), recent findings suggest that fostering feature persistence is crucial for solving geometric environments. We investigate this hypothesis by analyzing a single-game agent capable of completing multiple geometric tasks. We observe that although the agent solution appears simple, it is essentially a persistent representation. We further demonstrate hand that enhancing this persistence explicitly boosts performance. These findings have significant implications for designing persistent representations across RL applications.

We present a Newtonian extension of the Extended Ensemble Monte Carlo (EMMC) algorithm, implementing it on mesoscopic 3D dipolar models to explore phase transitions across system sizes ranging up to 500,000 particles. While confinement effects in numerical simulations typically prompt the use of this multiflange ESMC technique—preventing the "dynamical arrest" often encountered in Newtonian versions—we find that phase transitions in the ESMC approach closely parallel those observed in canonical ensemble. This Monte Carlo version effectively prevents dynamical phase coarsening, allowing for faster exploration of phase space. However, its lack of momentum-dependent thermodynamics prevents accurate modeling of wave propagation.

This paper addresses two primary issues in Sound Event Detection: data scarcity and class imbalance. We introduce DataMixing, a novel algorithm that enhances performance by augmenting data through the synthesis of mixed samples. This algorithm generates fused representations of overlapping samples, including those fully or partially overlapping, to capture overlapping characteristics for training classification models. This process boosts the effectiveness of detection while enhancing the separation of concurrent sources. Additionally, we evaluate various classifiers, demonstrating that the DataMixing approach combined with a gradient boosting machine yields state-of-the-art outcomes on specific tasks.

This work introduces the concept of a superposition scheme, demonstrating its efficacy in explaining properties such as randomized quantization, privacy preservation in federated learning, and non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA). Under this framework, a random linear combination of a deterministic vector and a random signal is defined as "superimposed." We prove that if two distinct vectors—each independently paired with its own unique random coding sequence—superimpose to yield identical results when multiplied with a single shared random code, then both original vectors must be recoverable. This result establishes the theoretical underpinning for applied scenarios, including feerated learning non-invasvE and NOMA techniques. Furthermore, we outline future directions for investigating the superimposition scheme, including the derivation of a lower bound on sample size in federated learning and the capacity analysis in NOMA.

This paper presents a novel theoretical framework for signal processing that integrates estimation and detection strategies within the theory of empirical level sets applied to spectrograms—a concept previously proposed by the current authors in \cite{KazMeiOya2019}. Specifically, estimation is achieved by identifying the empirical loss function's contour lines at specific quantile thresholds, while detection relies on verifying whether level sets exist at designated levels. We provide a rigorous mathematical proof demonstrating both the statistical optimality (especially regarding detection) and efficiency (estimation) of these level-set derived methods, subsequently establishing an estimation rate which serves as the foundation for estimation testing. These theoretical findings are complemented by extensive numerical experiments, which not only validate and illustrate our methods but also confirm the efficacy of the proposed approach when applied to various audio signals.

This study addresses the determination of synchronization clusters within a dynamical system and calculates their precise count. Through an algorithmic approach utilizing a directed heterogeneity graph, we reveal a deep connection between synchronization clusters and minimal spanning forests in the corresponding structure. Leveraging this relationship, the work determines the number of such clusters by analyzing the rank of a specific superimposed matrix associated with the dynamical system. Additionally, the paper introduces a algorithm capable of identifying individual synchronization clusters by processing binary comparison states. Numerical examples are provided to validate and demonstrate both methods.

We introduce a new module designed to simulate diverse physical systems, including particle movement governed by central forces and light ray deviation via geometric optics. Additionally, a relative motion scenario involving two bodies influenced by mutual gravitational attraction is demonstrated. This module was developed utilizing JavaFX and GNovatoL.

Although evidence indicates multiple flavors of El Niño and La Niña, research has predominantly examined the standard variants (ENSO34). This study investigates the oceanic and atmospheric characteristics, as well as precipitation outcomes, for both atypical eastern extreme events (EEs) and their counterparts. Our findings reveal distinct rainfall signatures in South America for these atypical events compared to ENSO34. Furthermore, divergent precipitation impacts from atypical events are observed across Asia and Africa. At an oceanic level, atypical events display unique patterns that diverge from those of ENSO34. Consequently, monitoring and modeling efforts should account for these unique signatures to improve accuracy in forecasting and climate analysis.

The accretion of supermassive black holes (BHs) in the early universe is widely attributed to direct gas collapse within protogalaxies, a mechanism that theoretically yields higher final BH masses compared to standard accretion from stellar remnant black holes formed via supernovae. In this study, we investigate how early-stage stellar BH formation can still produce heavy seeds capable of reaching supermassive status by protogalactic direct collapse, even after accounting for inefficiencies in stellar feedback. We apply semi-analytical techniques within a cosmological framework, modeling BH growth through protogalactic accretion under conditions where BH seeds are light. We demonstrate that inadequate galactic potential depth leads to excessive fragmentation of primordial gas clouds, resulting in lighter resulting BHs than if fragmentation were more constrained. Consequently, the mass function of these early BHs exhibits a flatter slope than previously predicted due to lower initial fragmentation. This early population of low-mass BHs can substantially contribute to supermassive BH growth via rapid accretion in the first billion years of the universe, resulting in a terminal black hole mass distribution that is skewed toward lower masses.

While flat band-induced correlated phenomena in two-dimensional kagome systems have attracted substantial research, establishing a robust flat band across the extensive kagome network presents significant challenges. Overcoming this obstacle requires overcoming intrinsic geometric constraints, as non-interacting kagome models rarely produce exactly flat bands. In this study, we demonstrate that distinct inter-orbital interactions within a honeycomb lattice of multi-orbital atoms can precisely neutralize the kinetic energy broadening caused by these interactions, thereby generating a true flat band. We investigate a three-orbital configuration involving in-plane d-orbitals arranged in a honeycomb geometry and employ both exact diagonalization and self-consistent mean-field methodologies to analyze correlation impacts. Our findings proceed from a Mott insulating phase at half-filling to metal-insulator transitions upon doping. Notably, at low doping levels, we observe the emergence of superconductivity, a superconducting state potentially driven by spin-fluctuation mechanisms and characterized by d-wave symmetry.

Phenotypic variation stems from complex interactions among genetic differences, environmental factors, and their interplay. Although identifying causal genetic variants for specific traits is crucial, these variants are often sparse relative to phenotypically relevant SNPs discovered through large-scale association analyses. We introduce a novel deep learning framework, Phenotype-SNN, designed to determine sequence-phenotype mappings by distinguishing phenotypic variations from SNP patterns while accounting for confounding factors. Applying this method to extensive datasets from the UK Biobank yielded two key findings: (1) the relationship between sequence and phenotypes is highly dynamic, as one sequence cannot consistently explain the same phenotypic variations across all traits, and (2) there is a strong correlation between proteins encoded by phenotypes and the locations of the underlying causal variants. Notably, when sequences involve numerous SNPs, the corresponding proteins often drive large changes between states. This suggests that proteins serve as effective functional anchors for interpreting large-scale phenotypic variations and their associated genetic variations. The source code is available on GitHub: https://github.com/yzhangzhang/Phenotype-SNN.

We introduce a strain entropy functional tailored to spin-polarized and unpolarized correlated electronic configurations within confined geometries. Derived from the Adamo and Gorling-Senzadhi functionals but enhanced to address nonlocal exchange and correlation correlation effects alongside Coulomb-hole influences. Derivatives of this functional yield orbital-optimized electronic structures which exhibit significant correspondence with external models. Notably, informational entropies associated with this framework capture Coulomb correlation behavior seen in specific confinement scenarios. Finally, illustrative results from diverse confinement models are discussed.

Using the Gaia Data Release 3, we have identified 131 wide binary systems with separations exceeding 1,000 au. A statistical analysis was conducted to determine the distance-dependent and wide-distance-dependent velocity dispersion for these pairs. We adopted an approach similar to that of Kervella et al. (2017) but integrated the individual line-of-sight velocities for each star, derived from Gaia's astrometric orbits, to enhance precision; this method also mitigates biases associated with binary orbital inclination. Additionally, to isolate true kinematic signals from orbital influences, we integrated motion corrections across various orbital parameters. The results indicate that applying line velocities enhances measurement accuracy by a factor of two to 30. While predicted trends showing decreasing velocity dispersion with increasing distance (and separation) were confirmed, these trends were found to be of statistically negligible importance for distances beyond 300 pc and very large separations. Finally, after removing the effects of wide binary skewness, our derived velocities align well with previous independent studies, yet remain consistently lower by approximately 2 km s⁻¹ compared to the values reported by Kervella et al. (2017).

In this work, we leverage deep learning techniques to either forecast the synchronization between specific pairs of financial time series or anticipate synchronization events within groups. While we demonstrate that our approach effectively identifies when certain pair alignments occur, we also highlight significant limitations: deep learning generally fails to predict such synchronization events for most series combinations, and it generally cannot forecast synchronization when the events are sparse in the data.

We employ fully non-adiabatic molecular dynamics simulations to examine how coherent quantum states within a metal atom influence surface-mediated atomistic processes, utilizing a quantum-mode-control model for a copper atom bound to copper surfaces. By coupling these quantum states coherently to specific vibrational modes, we achieve significant reductions in reaction barriers for scenarios ranging from metal atom welding to catalysis and vacancy formation. These findings offer essential insights for investigating reaction pathways and controlling chemistry at the quantum-level in metal systems.

Online advertising platforms utilize personalized ads to facilitate item sales, typically employing click-through rate (CTR) prediction models to forecast user engagement and maximize revenue. While existing CTR systems excel at capturing item characteristics and sequential user behavior, they often overlook individual item identities (visual IDs), despite significant performance variations among similar items. To address this gap, we introduce CTR4D, a multi-view CTR prediction framework for ad images that integrates visual feature extraction, sequence analysis, and item visual ID representation. Specifically, the visual ID module learns unique identities for each image through self-attention mechanisms, with learned ID features fused into traditional multi-view prediction layers. Evaluations utilizing large-scale industry data confirm the effectiveness of the visual ID strategy, establishing CTR4D as a robust and versatile solution for broad applicability in advertising.

This paper introduces the notion of projected constraints, adapting temporal logic to incorporate cardinality limits commonly found in business process modeling. Through various examples, the study highlights the specific challenges these constraints pose to the handling of concurrent actions. Furthermore, the work examines the decidability of satisfying these constraints and presents algorithms for their offline verification.

Wildfires represent a severe natural disaster, and their growth and trajectory are frequently influenced by atmospheric conditions. Consequently, the ability to forecast Airborne Oxide Particulate Deposition (AOD) from active fire zones is crucial for safeguarding public health. Within the fire boundary, chemical and physical interactions governing AOD formation are highly intricate; however, current physics-based forecast tools often lack adequate empirical foundation for the extreme conditions typical of fires, leading to potential inaccuracy. This study introduces a physics-informed statistical framework designed to enhance AOD propagation forecasting. Specifically, we employ a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) grounded in equations of atmospheric motion to generate predictions of AOD fields surrounding wildfires. We validate this methodology using CNN models trained on high-resolution Community Fire and Smoke Model (CFSM) simulations against which no real-world field evaluations have yet occurred. The findings demonstrate that this statistical CNN approach successfully predicts AOD distributions around fires more accurately than conventional physics-based standards evaluated without field data comparison, offering a viable solution for AOD estimation where traditional models fall short.

This paper introduces a framework designed to mitigate privacy risks in location-based services (LBS) arising from privacy disclosures related to conditionally dependent data. While prior approaches focused on independent data points, our method explicitly handles dependencies, ensuring that derived predictions for private locations are secure against inference attacks. To achieve this, our approach employs a Markov network to forecast conditionally dependent information and uses Bayesian optimization to selectively query dependent variables, thereby restricting disclosure only to the minimum necessary data required for accurate forecasts. We validated this framework using two real-world datasets, proving its ability to establish highly private yet precise data predictions.

Functional connectivity (FC) maps from neuroimaging are widely utilized to identify variations in neural network topology associated with various conditions. However, the extent to which these differences reflect genuine neural events, rather than artifacts of measurement noise, remains a critical unresolved issue. A recent study by Finn et al. (2015) highlighted that including spatially intersite effects in FC significantly enhances the ability to detect both individual and intersubject variability. We argue that this finding can be better understood by applying concepts from asymptotic theory for nonparametric estimators. Specifically, the inclusion of intersite dimensions in the FC similarity metric reduces the estimates' asymptotic variance, thereby yielding greater statistical power for distinguishing between subjects and groups. To further investigate how spatial aggregation influences FC reliability, we conducted simulations using realistic fMRI noise characteristics. These analyses demonstrated that while spatially aggregated data consistently outperforms unaggregated data across various scenarios, they also revealed a counterintuitive result: highly efficient estimators with minimum variance are not necessarily those that maximize the minimax estimation rate.

This review examines the connection between heat flow and the implementation of concentration of measure inequalities. It begins with the classical geometric probability framework and progresses through more intricate settings.

Positional encoding is a vital element of most pre-trained language models (PLMs), yet most current studies employ standard positional encodings that were designed exclusively for single-language, character-level inputs. These conventional encodings struggle to encode position effectively in code-mixed contexts, likely due to extreme variations in token lengths and vocabularies across different languages. To address this challenge, this paper introduces MLME-PTE, a novel positional encoding scheme tailored specifically for mixed-language texts. Additionally, we codified this mechanism as a plug-and-play modular component that can be integrated into various PLMs. The method was evaluated across three distinct datasets from two different languages and integrated with BERT, T5, and XLM-RoBERTa architectures. The results demonstrate that MLME-PTE consistently surpasses positional encodings using standard indexing methods across all dataset scenarios.

Subtle variations in individual genes drive the complex traits and evolution of complex organisms, with average impacts of gene substitutions typically guiding evolutionary trajectories rather than isolated rare events. Consequently, tracking phenotypic changes necessitates understanding this prevalence of average effects. This study investigates how average effects evolve within a rigorous mathematical framework featuring two core assumptions: (1) phenotypes result from multiple interacting genes, and (2) gene substitutions cause small phenotypic shifts. Under these conditions, if interactions are limited in both range and number, we demonstrate that an isolated island population's gene substitutions lead to cumulative phenotypic change dominated by an average effect that remains nearly constant regardless of which specific genes are replaced. This holds true within a model population initially in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium and possessing additive gene interactions. Furthermore, if a migrating stream of genetically similar individuals enters such a population, mixing with the locals to form a new group also exhibits this steady phenotypic average per gene substitution. This insight illuminates long-standing concepts, including the concept of "mutational vulnerability," and extends them through a formal derivation, suggesting a general rule: even with localized interactions between genes, most evolutionary progress can be explained by average effects when those interactions are relatively short.

Bipedal robots, though capable of executing complex tasks, typically lack sufficient stability due to inherent dynamical instabilities, resulting in ineffective use of redundant degrees of freedom to enhance stability. This study introduces a novel closed-loop, experimentally validated biodynamic feedback controller for human-like bipedal locomotion on flat surfaces. Unlike standard open-loop controllers, this method integrates sensory feedback after every step during steady-state walking to dynamically adjust controller parameters. By forming a feedback controller based on measured kinematic states, the gait loop is closed, allowing the system to self-correct and maintain stability. Experimentally, this approach demonstrates a capability to adapt step lengths and frequencies on the go based on online controller parameter shifts. These real-time adaptations, unattainable through pre-planned open-loop strategies, serve as a critical test for validating this controller's utility. Ultimately, this study establishes a new control paradigm for significantly improving bipedal robot stability by leveraging human-inspired, real-time adaptive strategies.

Personalized federated learning (LFL) addresses client heterogeneity by enabling tailored model adaptations for individual users. Although semi-unsupervised approaches have been employed to utilize clients' unlabeled data, these methods often rely on assumptions that cause overfitting in clients limited to small amounts of labeled data. To mitigate this, we introduce a novel personalization framework incorporating semi-supervised techniques that focuses specifically on clients with high-label data scarcity. By incorporating clients' labeled data into semi-unsupervised personalization, we enhance initial model performance for these limited-data users. To further boost accuracy, we construct a supervised loss function that incorporates pseudo-labels generated from unlabeled data. Additionally, we integrate regularization terms based on both supervised and unsupervised losses to mitigate overfitting in clients lacking abundant labels. Empirical results indicate that our method significantly surpasses existing personalized federated learning approaches, particularly for clients limited to small amounts of labeled data.

Neutron star–neutron star (NS-NS) mergers generate magnetic fields within the accretion disk that undergo significant evolution following neutron star disruption. We investigate this disk magnetic field development in NS-NS coalescence events utilizing full-3D general relativistic magnetohydrodynamics (GRMHD) simulations. In our model model, initial disks with a mean disk magnetic field of roughly $10^{-4}$ relative to the equipartition level develop within seconds after disruption. During this initial phase, the mean field remains stable over time. However, on longer timescales of a minute, the field exhibits rapid growth. This evolution is driven by dynamic phenomena including disk ejections and holes formation which lead to concentrated magnetic flux. The simultaneous emergence of holes and intense magnetic islands boosts the mean field strength by one to two orders of magnitude within minutes. These dynamics significantly alter the properties of the newly formed disk and the resulting evolutionary path of the system.

This investigation examines the dynamics of conditional dynamics within Markov processes restricted to specific subsets of their state space, characterized by an absorbing mechanism that transitions to the subset's exterior. Under stronger strong Feller conditions combined with a logarithmic strong irreducibility hypothesis, the analysis further achieves a precise large-deviation principle governing the asymptotic behavior of the absorption time's rate function.

In this study, equilibrium configurations of graphene-based capacitors containing dielectric materials are investigated using density functional theory. It is found that altering the graphene chemical potential shifts the stable positions of the adsorbed dipole and cubic dielectric particles toward states with lower total energy. Specifically, a logarithmic relationship exists between the magnitude of the carbon–carbon bond length in the free single-layer graphene sheet and its chemical potential. Additionally, the particle location within the center of the nonbonding region of an isolated layer can be precisely controlled by varying this potential. The authors also explore how adatom incorporation into graphene influences the stability of these dielectric particles.

Even though length of stay in the Emergency Department (ED) serves as a performance indicator, increasing efficiency simply to reduce patient wait times may compromise the quality of care. To address whether efficiency gains might inadvertently increase system congestion and patient demand, this study examines the relationship between patient throughput efficiency and ED visits using 2015 data from over 300 U.S. hospitals. By employing difference-in-differences analysis, we examine variations in effiicency driven by the implementation of new information technology that enhanced real-time patient tracking. Results indicate that improving efficiency—defined as reducing the time required to discharge or transfer a patient—was associated with higher efficiency in attracting patients over the following year, even after accounting for facility and regional controls. Furthermore, for hospital system affiliates, our findings reveal that efficiency improvements led to noticeably higher 30-day ED revisit and readmission rates, with statistical and economic significance observed in the added ED visits and hospital admissions respectively. These associations appear robust across various subgroups, including different patient demographics, but were not detected for standalone hospitals. Ultimately, these results suggest that enhancing ED efficiency may accelerate the flow of patients back to the hospital, thereby elevating both revisit frequencies and admission costs.

This study investigates the impact of a varying difficulty distribution for tasks on how agents—individually or collectively—should approach decision-making. This paper introduces FedIDS, an anony-mous federated learning framework for network intrusion detection. We introduce a new parallel task scheduling approach rooted in biologically inspired concepts, specifically focusing on how organisms manage internal organ coordination during movement. Rather than relying on simulation-based learning, which can be inefficient, we schedule tasks based on the specific hardware of the robot in question, allowing for greater hardware adaptation. Additionally, we developed a new biologically inspired motion primitive called "sculpting," which refines existing techniques by more effectively coordinating the robot's degrees of freedom to relationship with external objects. Unlike sculpting, which focuses solely on relationship-based coordination, our proposed method also considers how the motion of one part of the environment can be predicted based on other parts of that same environment's current state.

The performance of short-channel semiconductor devices is fundamentally tied to the mobility of charge carriers. Using Silicon Nitride (Si3N4) as a gate material example, we analyze how this selection impacts device performance anisotropy. Furthermore, we analyze correlations between work function induced bandgap bending and mobility anisotropy. Ultimately, these findings offer guidance for selecting appropriate gate materials to maintain efficient short-channel control.

Semisupervised Node Classification (SNLC) aims to predict labels for nodes lacking annotations within a network, leveraging available labels and the structure of the graph. To mitigate this, we introduce POLE-GNN, a novel framework designed to produce reliable pseudo labels through a novel probability optimization mechanism. Specifically, this approach refines model predictions by balancing the probabilities of both high and low confidence classes, effectively filtering out unreliable assessments. Our experiments across various datasets indicate that this advanced method substantially outperforms current state-of-the-art solutions in scenarios involving limited labeling.

We introduce PatchNet, a lightweight neural network designed for object instance segmentation within video clips, with Object Segmentation in Motion (OMM) as the specific task. Despite this efficiency, it maintains robust performance, recording an Average Precision (AP) of 48.6. Running at an speed of 109.5 frames per second (fps) on an OMAP499 processor, PatchNet delivers industry-leading real-time segmentation results.

GPs are frequently employed to model and forecast complex, multivariate spatial phenomena, such as temperature or rainfall patterns. Standard practice involves using multiple GP instances, where specific realizations are fixed based on observed data; however, this approach leaves conditional relationships between these distinct processes somewhat ambiguous. Within a graphical model framework, one might aim to construct separate GP processes so that, after conditioning on a shared set of observations, they become mutually independent. Achieving this requires defining a structure where, in a visual graph representation, distinct GP processes are separated by nodes rather than being connected via edges, thereby preventing direct interactions between realizations that have not been conditioned upon. This work presents a methodology for formulating marginal constraints and conditional independence structures using multiple GP processes through a multivariate formulation. Specifically, multiple covariates are defined for each of the constituent GP processes, where some remain latent. Setting appropriate sparsity within these latent variables effectively decimates the two realizations in graphical models while preserving the specified independence and maintaining valid correlations among specific realizations. This technique facilitates more rigorous interpretation of how different processes relate one another and allows for targeted modeling of interactions based on domain expertise.

This study introduces the Generalized Chebyshev method (GCM), an optimization algorithm designed to minimize quadratic-approximated objectives based on Newton's approach. Moiré heterostructures have attracted significant research attention due to their tunable and customizable electronic landscapes, which have led to a diverse array of exotic quantum phases. Correspondingly, optical spectroscopy has emerged as a vital tool for characterizing these systems, with theoretical models providing robust support. This study introduces a comprehensive framework that unifies optical characteristics with electronic structures in moiré heterostructures, leveraging a tight-binding approach to compute interlayer exciton band structures and optical transitions. We developed a method to solve the two-dimensional Schrödinger equation for excitons by incorporating parabolic band dispersions for both electron and hole bands, alongside their charge-neutral interaction potentials. The resulting optical spectra are unit cell-resolved, offering a direct correlation between interlayer exciton binding energies—limited by the interlayer Coulomb force—and measured exciton dispersion. These findings confirm that optical spectra are most effectively described as sidebands of the exciton dispersion, situated near the moiré superlattice's energy minima and maxima. Specifically, for thiol-functionalized transition metal dichalcogenide moiré heterostructures, optical spectra primarily reflect the interlayer exciton dispersion and its associated binding energy. This approach is universally applicable to diverse excitonic materials and can be adapted to study other charged-neutral interactions within such systems.

This paper presents the development of a probabilistic data association algorithm equipped with adaptive features that enhance position tracking for mobile units undergoing adaptive constant velocity motion while navigating a time-varying obstacle course. The core mechanism involves an adaptive probabilistic data association (PDA) filter embedded within a grid-based cell algorithm, where the underlying probabilistic framework is modified to support bidirectional associations between the filter and the sensor. Additionally, grid-based cells are bidirectional linked to facilitate mutual position updates across the system. This approach is grounded in a generalized PDA filter operating within interconnected grid cells, which incorporates a variable grid size and an adaptive state transition model designed to minimize estimation uncertainty.

Interior point methods (IPMs) are among the most popular tools for numerical optimization. A significant advancement in these methods is early termination of inner loops, a strategy demonstrated to accelerate solving large-scale problems by enabling them to stop before reaching full precision at every step while still finding optimal results within an acceptable tolerance. Previous research applied this to fully polynomial-time interior point schemes, showing beneficial outcomes. Our contribution adapts this early termination approach to barrier parameter methods (BPMs), another prominent class of IPMs known for their practical success. By extending existing theoretical frameworks, this paper demonstrates that preserving polynomial-time guarantees for barrier parameter methods remains viable even with early termination.

An AI system's capability to succeed in real-world scenarios is defined by its capacity to handle diverse, often unpredictable challenges. As AI integration expands, it is crucial to analyze and learn from AI failures to improve current architectures and streamline the development process. The AI Incident Database (https://aiddatabase.org/) serves as a centralized, searchable repository for reports regarding AI failures and control issues. By providing detailed accounts of problems affecting both industrial and consumer AI, the database allows developers to extract insights that streamline the creation of intelligent systems. Ultimately, this tool supports research aimed at artificial resilience and intelligent agency. We anticipate that tool will gain wider utility among the engineering community focused on machine intelligence.

We introduce a gauge invariant, non-linear differential equation for the Evolution Renormalization Group (EVG) that results from merging an exact RG flow with a specific resummation of coupled Bethe-Salpeter equations specific to the non-abelian gauge theory. This framework provides a closure for the RG invariant differential equation. After performing a numerical solution in both $D=4$ and $D=3$ spacetime, we demonstrate that this approach upholds gauge invariance within Yang-Mills theory. Furthermore, we analyze the implications of these results for symmetry breaking and mass generation mechanisms.

This paper introduces a novel on-the-fly monitoring algorithm designed to provide real-time feedback on conformance across multiple process models simultaneously. Our system supports the comparison of execution traces against various formal specifications, including workflow models based on control flow and business processes focusing solely on best practices. To effectively handle potential conflicts or conflicts between specifications, our design employs a mechanism to provide several recommendations. To ensure that all recommendations are valid with respect to the set of monitored processes, our solution utilizes a proposed algorithm that suggests valid next activities regardless of branch selection. Additionally, to accommodate practical scenarios where monitoring data may conflict with defined rules, our system includes an algorithm capable of generating explanations for conformance feedback through a process that highlights which specifications were violated. Our solution is fully automatic in its execution and does not require manual intervention to generate conformance explanations with effort. To demonstrate the utility of this system, our solution was applied to a business process and best practice monitoring scenario that involved analyzing workflow data from a company.

We introduce an extension to the quantum-HoC abstract machine specifically designed to preserve quantum cloning restrictions. This implementation rests on two pivotal concepts: (1) representing quantum states as first-class PrO-Quipper-M data structures and ( (2) utilizing "qflags" to enforce a no-cloning policy. While our approach naturally introduces several theoretical nuances, real-world classical metadata can often fill these gaps practically. We demonstrate this feasibility with a classical-aided implementation of crucial operations like quantum measurements and entangled Bell states. This work thereby bridges the theoretical requirements of operational QC language PR O Quipper-M to build practical, clone resistant programming constructs in OpQuipper model (2).

Furthermore, this approach offers valuable insights into the nontrivial corrections observed in related systems, such as the GUE orthogonal ensemble and the Jac en ensemble.

This research investigates quantum-enhanced optical phase sensing using quantum-correlated light, specifically investigating how a freely adjustable phase rotator can induce controllable interconversion between amplitude and phase quadratures in two-mode squeezed vacuum states. These characteristics facilitate a novel phase sensing scheme that employs the two-mode squeezed amplitude state, enabling measurement backaction evasion through the use of large-amplitude inputs which suppresses backaction. We demonstrate that measuring these large-amplitude squeezed quadratures allows for arbitrarily precise phase determination with potential sensitivity improvements of up to 10 dB, achievable via quantum-correlated light compared to standard coherent beams for which no quantum correlations exist. These findings suggest that quantum-correlated light not only supports quantum-enhanced sensing but also facilitates measurement backaction avoidance through elegant solutions involving quantum-flux evasion.

Multiway number partitioning serves as a fundamental computational problem with wide-ranging applications in bioinformatics, including vector ranking and generalizing two-way number partitioning for genomic sequence assembly. Ultimately, the edge errors are calculated using Lp norms across different Lp values through a local strategy using O(GlogN) operations on N elements in a graph containing G edges, with the specific case for Lp=2 achieving this via the local distribution of the normal O(G+N) operations on N elements in the graph with G edges.

We employ angular clustering statistics derived from the 2021 Lointess Observatory Sky Survey (LoTSS) first data release to test the $\Lambda$CDM model using 200+ degree two-point correlation functions and quadrupole moments. These analyses were executed for galaxies brighter than specific flux limits across the $140 \leq\log\leq 15.5$ magnitude range spanning $-14 \leq z\leq 1402$ angular scales in arcminutes. While our findings align with $\Lambda$CDM predictions, significant systematics remain; specifically, the failure to model the extragalactic background light (EBLK) introduces a 10–20 per cent legacy error for scales below 10 arcminutes. Additionally, while no single power-law model adequately describes the full dataset, we identify a distinct break in the correlation function at approximately 15 arcminutes ($\sim 15Gpc h^{-1}$), a feature likely attributable to galaxies at high redshifts ($z \gtrsim 150.150$). Finally, we contrasted these results with predictions based on a wCDE model featuring a dynamically evolving equation-of-state parameter, finding that such an extension to the standard cosmological framework yielded no statistically significant deviations from the standard model.

The high-dimensional rank lasso problem involves minimizing a sum of ranks combined with an $\ell_1$-norm regularizer. Leveraging the theory of alternating direction methods, this approach enjoys linear convergence rates. Furthermore, incorporating a gradient-sum technique allows the method to minimize a convex-concave objective specifically designed to handle ranks efficiently. Empirical results indicate that our algorithm converges rapidly and generates robust estimations of significant practical relevance.

This study explores the potential Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) holds for quantifying the environmental impacts of AI services and investigating the relationship between performance metrics like latency and carbon footprint. To address the challenge of data collection, we introduce a framework designed to gather LCA results for AI services at a large scale. Using this tool, we conducted an LCA assessment of 22 prominent LLM inference processes across various model families, including comparisons of model sizes, which revealed distinct variations in environmental impact among models of identical types but different scales, yet relatively minor differences among other model families. Furthermore, we developed a mathematical model that accurately links a service's latency to its total environmental footprint. Findings from this model demonstrate that increasing computational power to reduce latency may backfire; in many scenarios, the environmental gains are negated. Consequently, the data suggests that LCA offers a practical method for linking specific AI services to their environmental impacts. This insight supports both policy-making within tech companies and corporate decision-making, enabling a more sustainable future where AI technology operates in harmony with ecological limits.

Prescriptive process monitoring suggests optimal future actions aimed at confining deviations to normal operating ranges. Although numerous proposed methods demonstrate effective results within experimental or controlled simulated environments, their applicability in real-world scenarios remains unassessed, a gap this study addresses. The research introduces a novel evaluation technique for these prescriptive methods by utilizing a case study on a completed, actual production process case that experienced significant delays. The study compares the recommendations of existing approaches against historical data to determine which suggestions are both feasible and beneficial for process improvement; furthermore, it proposes a specific metric to quantify the advantage of each method's recommendations. Through this analysis, the study establishes the foundations for prescriptive process monitoring in practical applications and offers a novel assessment standard for developing these methods.

The governing equations employ a large eddy simulation (LES) framework combined with a desingularized force formulation derived from potential flow theory. The implementation details of the connection between a potential flow technique providing desingularized body forces and the LES are featured. Furthermore, an adaptive algorithm driven by a dual-weighted residual error assessment is employed to locally refine the mesh. The methodology was validated through tests on basic ship models, contrasting numerical results against established experimental datasets and resistance estimations derived from potential flow analyses.

This study examines the formation of opinion clusters within an opinion-division framework, where individuals possess one-dimensional stances and encounter two distinct behaviors: oscillation between opposing views or convergence toward a consensus. We demonstrate that, at the macro level, these dynamics result in social segmentation. Our analysis provides an opinion-division specific extension of classical results by Holme and Saramaki [1] and Holub [1]—previously limited to static results involving purely attractive or purely repulsive interactions—by accommodating both oscillatory and consensus-forming preference structures. We present exact theoretical results and simulation-based findings, which collectively confirm that local clustering is inevitable. Notably, the experimental data indicate an indeterminate nature to the resulting opinion-division social segmentation.

This analysis examines both equilibrium and non-equilibrium dynamics of perturbations within black holes adorned with scalar hair, a phenomenon also prevalent in holographic superconductor models. We examine the properties of linear, time-dependent, infinitesimal distortions in isolated systems, as well as hydrodynamic corrections to impedance during near-perfect conductivity transitions and viscous fluid flows coupled with abelian gauge fields. A significant finding is the emergence of diffusive modes involving viscous motion of the fluid and shear channels driven by minimal coupling. We extend these findings into more complex scenarios, incorporating finite viscosity, scattering experiments involving scalars and gravitons against moving surfaces with reflective characteristics, as well as black holes with rotating characteristics endowed with scalar hair and viscous fluid backgrounds. In these contexts, we elucidate a dual relationship explaining the connection between observables of dissipators without spontaneous symmetry breakdown and those exhibiting spontaneous symmetry breakdown.

Temperature serves as a critical factor in biological reactions, and its fluctuations can impact the timing of gene expression by altering protein production rates. This study examines how cells might utilize variability in mRNA synthesis times as a mechanism for adaptation to environmental changes. Even in generic promoters, temperature fluctuations affect transcription finish times and the eventual emergence of mature mRNA. By coupling stochastic fluctuations in protein creation with steepest-ascent optimization, we demonstrate that organisms can exploit these temperature-driven variations in mRNA maturation timing to refine phenotypes. Furthermore, by analyzing protein production variability, we propose that protein levels act as indicators of physiological temperature history. Lastly, we propose an adaptation strategy involving genes of varying lengths; this allows cells to generate diverse mRNA production times from a single transcript using only basic regulatory adjustments, thereby enabling faster acclimation to changing environments through a specific number of protein copies.

This work investigates mixed gauge-gravity anomalies and pure gravitational anomalies in $SU(N)$ gauge theories featuring an odd number of fundamental fermion flavors. By introducing additional Weyl fermions in the adjoint representation, we demonstrate that these anomalies can be eliminated through a specific chirality configuration of gravitational fermions. Consequently, we establish a consistent framework constructing non-perturbative $SU(N)$ quantum gravity theories with an arbitrary number of fundamental fermion flavors.

In this paper, we purport that for all group codes $C$ and $D$ such that $D \supseteq C$, then code equivalence exists between $D/D^\perp$ and $C$. This finding extends that of their earlier work.

Optimization and inference in graphical models are fundamentally constrained by the largest induced width throughout the computation. This limitation can be significantly mitigated using Bucket Elimination, a straightforward variation of dynamic programming that yields functions featuring limited domain sizes—specifically, at most the bucket's original size minus one. By integrating data-driven heuristics that evaluate and rank intermediate results, we can prioritize paths that maintain smaller bucket widths. This paper introduces an adaptation of Bucket Elimination that selectively computes these limited-sized intermediate functions, thereby enhancing both optimization and inference efficiency. We examine how to assess potential branches, outlining a data-centric approach that leverages local model structure versus a scoring mechanism based on local data that draws from already processed buckets. These heuristics prove effective in reducing computational demands, as demonstrated by an adapted bucket-dropping version of dynamic belief updating, as evidenced by experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are increasingly applied to integrate sensory data across diverse research fields. This research examines physics-based inference in identifying objects that are dropped from varying heights. We propose using principles of physical free-fall to guide a neural network, enabling the prediction of drop object identity from sensor measurements. We tested two physics-informed models: one based on the equation of motion and another utilizing an attention mechanism aligned with physical equations. We also compared these approaches against a conventional machine learning model and an alignment-free attention technique. We collected datasets using a droplet detector equipped with microphones and a high-speed camera, and conducted a rigorous evaluation by testing on data from multiple locations and for different object types. We found that models trained with our collected data and generalized through their physical knowledge outperformed standard machine learning algorithms. Furthermore, the physics-integrated frameworks demonstrated greater reliability when validating against drop scenarios from higher elevations and novel object materials compared to methods lacking explicit physical alignment.

Recent research has identified frictionless isotropic jamming in discrete systems featuring long-range forces, distinguishing it from the conventional frictional shear jamming induced by external compression; however, a clear framework for characterizing the force- and strain-displacement correlations near the glass transition from a statistical mechanics standpoint has been absent. Addressing this gap, this study analyzes a generalized model incorporating joint constraints in both space and force domains, enabling the investigation of the interplay between friction and jamming. By employing molecular dynamics simulations on the resulting dense amorphous packings, we observe that the system undergoes a transition to an isothermal jammed state at a specific critical separation depth ($z_c$) lacking a reliance on a power-law scaling in the hyperbolic constraint. Furthermore, we differentiate between the scenarios of frictionless isotropic jamming and frictional shear jamming by comparing their critical exponents: the former yields $\gamma=2$ and $\delta=2$, whereas the latter presents $\gamma=3$ and $\delta=3$. These findings are corroborated by mean-field analysis and a proposed statistical mechanics framework featuring a generalized non-equilibrium free energy density expressed as $\tilde F = \frac{1}{2}\rho u + \frac{1}{V_c}\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{1}{F_{c,i}}F_{c,i}^2 + \frac{1}{2}u^2 + \tilde U$.

This study introduces an enhanced MS-AR(4) framework tailored for modeling daily electricity demand dynamics within the United Kingdom. An MS-AR(4) model integrates a seasonal mean with an autoregressive component of order 4, reflecting the understanding that demand decomposes into a long-term seasonal pattern and short-term temporal dependencies. In contrast, standard autoregressive models struggle to capture these seasonal fluctuations effectively. Although daily demand generally follows seasonal patterns influenced by time of year and daylight duration, current methods fall short in quantifying how climate-driven seasonal effects interact with daily demand dynamics.

To bridge this gap, we propose a novel methodology to estimate the sensitivity of daily electricity demand to weather conditions across different seasons. Leveraging sensitive meteorological data, including granular humidity readings obtained recently, we demonstrate how these factors impact demand dynamics. Our findings indicate a substantial decline in daily electricity demand during the spring and summer months of the calendar year.

To assist in identifying these biases without requiring technical AI expertise, we developed a user-centric framework employing a private Wikipedia-based LLM to assess public policy-related queries. Through two laboratory studies utilizing human participants, the framework demonstrated efficacy in bringing to light visibility biases—an issue previously under-researched—that favor commercial entities and advocacy groups while obscuring governmental sources. This approach offers a practical method for ensuring fairness in public policy information presentation.

This work introduces a frame-based, iterative program synthesis framework designed to solve the Skolemization challenge in first-order logic programs containing recursion. Our method leverages Python's capability for dynamic programming generation, creating and refining iterative solutions iteratively guided by the search for fixed points of operational predicates alongside carefully crafted domain constraints. Furthermore, we derive conditions under which our method guarantees terminating synthesis for programs of specific programizations.
