Compositional data consists of high-dimensional vectors subject to two constraints: all elements must be non-negative, and their sum must equal a fixed constant. Because these features render standard Euclidean geometry inappropriate, analysts typically employ "log-ratio" transformations to the data components. Highly interlinked variables frequently arise in this framework; thus, Constrained Principal Component Analysis (CPCA) has been introduced to extract meaningful dimensions while accounting for these interactions. This study investigates the spectral properties of CPCA by linking it to the computation of eigenlines within a uniform measure on the simplex. We demonstrate that both the number of significant output dimensions and the corresponding loadlines converge with high probability as the principal components of the transformed data that do not relate to a common ratio. In the limit, the largest out-of-sample principal dimensions are approximated by the empirical spectral distribution line, which approaches that predicted asymptotically in terms of a population covariance line. Finally, we provide theoretical approaches for inferential confidence intervals which may approach the sample dimensions of non-asymptotic error bounds.

The core-accretion theory predicts a specific distribution for gas giant exoplanets based on when runaway gas accretion begins relative to the growth of the dust core. While this model aligns well with predictions for gas-rich systems ($M_{\rm p} \gtrsim 60 M_{\rm Jup}$), it predicts fewer intermediate-mass planets ($M_{\rm p} \sim 30 M_{\rm Jup}$) than what observations show. We demonstrate that initiating runaway gas accretion with only slightly super-critical sound conditions yields a planet mass distribution matching observations across the $M_{\rm p} \gtrsim 30 M_{\rm Jup}$ and $M_{\rm p} \lesssim 30 M_{\rm Jup}$ regimes. We further prove that matching the actual number of massive planets requires launching runaway phases that are marginally critical, whereas a fully self-similar model predicts too many intermediate-mass planets and thus fails to resolve the discrepancy. Consequently, specific physics must trigger the onset of runaway gas accretion with near-critical sound conditions to account for the observed diversity of exoplanet masses.

A central challenge for artificial intelligence is navigating environments where interactions are partially observable. In these scenarios, agents must infer unobserved elements of their surroundings to formulate effective strategies. This paper introduces a dynamic memory architecture designed to construct a latent state representation, enabling agents to infer hidden information and refine predictions based on incomplete data. By integrating this architecture with deep reinforcement learning, we evaluate the method in both a partial observability setting and total state observability. Specifically, we focus on controlling Brownian motion and a deeper movement model, as well as predicting future trends in financial time series. The findings demonstrate that this flexible memory framework facilitates powerful learning across these distinct tasks.

We examine a well-motivated dark matter candidate generated via a SUGRA-mediated mechanism capable of resolving the $125\,\mathrm{GeV}$ Higgs boson's mass issues. This model offers compelling testable predictions, including potential signals of a $C\text{-}$odd scalar or pseudoscalar state within the $[100, 500]\,\mathrm{GeV}$ mass spectrum. When the mediator is much lighter than the dark matter particle ($\sim 100$ times less), the corresponding coupling must be extremely small ($\sim 10^{-4}$), enabling a lifetime extending up to $\sim 10^{20}$ seconds. Conversely, if the mediator exceeds the dark matter mass, at least two production channels become accessible at hadron colliders. Furthermore, if the mediator surpasses $\sim 500$ GeV, their coupling must be strong, resulting in a broad resonance that significantly corrects vacuum stability, thereby mandating a tuned Higgs mass.

A modified version of the standard battery used to measure cognitive impairment, referred to here as Mod-Cog (short for the Modified and Extended Battery of Cognitive Assessment), was developed by extending and expanding existing tasks to increase their complexity and diversity of cognitive functions. Mod-Cog retains three established tasks—Letter-Number Sequence, Symbol Trail, and Letter Word Test—but introduces three additional assessments: Modified Letter-Number Sequence, Enhanced Symbol Trail, and Revised Letter Word Test, each employing personalized test parameters. Participants underwent both versions, undergoing baseline assessments followed by three training sessions involving either an enhanced or modified battery protocol, followed by baseline re-assessment. Following this training, individuals were randomly assigned groups to participate in further interventions using one version or the other over four further training sessions, followed by a final evaluation phase at battery discharge. Mod-Cog demonstrated superior sensitivity to patient distinctions compared to its extended counterpart, exhibiting greater reliability with a stronger correlation between inter-rater scores. Furthermore, training efficacy was version-dependent rather than version-independent; specifically, training utilizing modified versions produced significantly greater improvements in both enhanced and other conditions than did modification training alone. These findings suggest that both versions offer distinct training advantages over non-modified methods, with enhanced versions yielding greater improvements than do modifications themselves, thereby validating further exploration into further refinement strategies within these batteries.

The paper examines radiation generated by the inverse Compton scattering of Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) photons by relativistic electrons within jet material. Findions from previous studies of the CMB inverse Compton effect in jet halos are applied to M87 and 3C279, highlighting how the relativistic motion of the jet expands the effective cross-section for this interaction. The results are categorized into two categories: first, the Doppler-boosted enhancement of the scattering geometric cross-section increases scattering probability; second, the motion of the jet produces a headlight effect that shifts scattered radiation to higher energies. These effects are evaluated in light of previous observations of CMB inverse Compton (IC) radiation in halo environments. The study concludes that for M87, CMB IC radiation is detectable only in cases where the jet is nearly aligned with the observer's view, as opposed to the more widespread detectability seen in non-relativistic halo scenarios. Conversely, for 3C279, nearly all jet material moving at relativistic speeds and contributing to CMB IC radiation is funneled into a narrow cone directed along the observer's line of sight. The paper finishes by suggesting that this mechanism could account for compact flares in radio galaxies and luminous variability in quasars.

We introduce and examine a 'pre-non-relativistic' parametrization designed to enable analytical expansion orders in general relativity by formally ccaling on $c$. Adopting isomorphic forms across the Einstein, Poisson, and Special Relativity frameworks and employing them specifically for further expansion in the Special Relativity context, we derive several key outcomes: we recover general relativistic expressions for the energy momentum tensor and gravitational self energy; we recover post Newtonian energy equations; and we obtain formulas for gravitational mass energy equivalence and inertia

We introduce SIFT-CPD, a novel algorithm for robust image registration that integrates SIFT feature matching with the DCP framework (DCP: Diffeable Correspondence and Projects). While DCP offers a robust, closed-form analytic solution for non-rigid alignment based on landmark features, its effectiveness is often limited by noise, inhomogeneous intensity contrast, and local pathologies—common issues prevalent in medical imaging. To address these constraints, our SIFT-CPD method initially identifies corresponding features using matched SIFT descriptors, subsequently feeding these coordinates into the DCP framework to calculate a smooth, reversible deformation field. We validated the algorithm's efficacy through experiments on synthetic data and diverse datasets comprising CT, MR, and optical microscopy scans. Comparative analyses against two established methods—STAB-FLW and conventional DCP—demonstrate that SIFT-CPD achieves superior performance in complex scenarios, particularly when aligning images with entirely dissimilar intensity profiles or regions containing abnormal structures.

This study introduces a framework based on Unsupervised Optimal Transport (UOT) designed to enhance cross-lingual embeddings and multi-lingual classification systems. First, we demonstrate that UOT-pooled descriptors yield superior results for image classification, enabling more effective cross-domain and cross-lingual alignment. Leveraging this insight, we propose UOT-Pooling as a novel layer to boost standard single-language neural networks, often matching or surpassing the efficacy of data augmentation strategies. Subsequently, we develop UOT-AOT-Pooling specifically for word representation; we apply single-instance optimization algorithms to calculate the optimal attention mechanism, yielding words representations that improve both intrinsic and intrinsic-to-extrinsic evaluation metrics. Finally, we employ these multi-lingual word descriptors within a UOT-Pooling framework to construct enhanced word vectors, effectively elevating classification accuracy across both low- and high-volume languages.

We investigate the relationship between the host galaxy's spiral structure and the orientation of nuclear Seyferts, utilizing UVCANS simulations. These simulations randomly scatter spherical or flattened emitters along spiral arms of various types within disc galaxies. The study demonstrates that type 1 and type 2 nuclei appear with contrasting orientation distributions at the centers of type A/B/C1 spiral galaxies, yet type C2 spiral hosts regulate the distribution differently based on spiral arm density. Only in systems featuring low-density arms do type 1 and type 2 objects display distinct orientation preferences, whereas a pronounced spiral arm density tends to equalize their distributions. These findings imply that host galaxies of grand-design or nearly symmetric spirals may harbor no visible AGNs, as strong spiral patterns scatter all nuclei such that both type 1 and type 2 observers see similar counts. Furthermore, simulations suggest that the discrepancy in AGN unification between spiral and elliptical galaxies stems from scattering mechanics: while density waves scatter nuclei differently in spirals (yielding distinct orientations), elliptical galaxies scatter emitters more uniformly to produce similar counts for both types.

This paper defines the pointwise 1-general map in general pointwise $1-n$ points on general rotation. Using this map of Gaussian characteristics for flat general rotational bodies to effect verification is achieved. Additionally, a revised general characteristic for flat general rotation is offered.

Although self-supervised deep learning methods for representing scenes have advanced significantly, they predominantly rely on image classification and pseudo-label generation, which are often not general-purpose. In this study, we introduce an alternative framework based on scene geometry estimation pre-training, specifically evaluating the effectiveness of predicting photometric consistency across translated images as a guide for generalization. To optimize these translations, we employ a variational autoencoder (VAE) equipped with a translation prior, allowing us to generate invariant representations derived from optical flow, depth, and translated image consistency. However, given the ill-posed nature of predicting 3D scene geometry, we argue that structural prediction tasks may yield superior generalization compared to classification. Consequently, our method generates synthetic image pairs featuring translations in position and position/depth by leveraging a scene synthesis model. We test these learned representations on generalization benchmarks, including synthetic pose shifts and real-world image translations, demonstrating competitive performance against established state-of-the-art self-supervised techniques.

The recent surge in Internet of Things (IoT) applications has generated a vast volume of time-series data. Nonetheless, translating this vast amount of data into annotated examples suitable for training machine learning models remains expensive and labor-intensive. To mitigate this limitation, we developed **TCube**, which enables the automatic design and self-training of adaptive models directly from unlabeled time-series data. By leveraging specialized tools for identifying and correcting imperfect transductive labels, **TCube** produces superior dataset annotations. Our approach offers three primary advantages: first, it eliminates the need for costly manual annotation; second, it enables continuous model adaptation to shifting data distributions; and third, it enhances labeling by incorporating both feature engineering and weak supervision strategies. Empirical results demonstrate that **TCube** significantly improves modeling accuracy for critical tasks such as classification, prediction, and anomaly detection.

In 2003, a novel recurrent neural network approach named Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) emerged in 2003. In 2014, Hason et al. demonstrated that applying this method to Japanese word segmentation could achieve accuracy surpassing handcrafted methods. This study aims to analyze the factors contributing to success so that Japanese word segmentation can be enhanced. To this end, we conducted an empirical study on feature engineering and feature selection. We evaluated various combinations of features by applying different selection strategies to three distinct LSTMs and observed their correlation with segmentation performance. Findings indicate that an optimal feature subset exists beyond our current exploration, suggesting further improvement is attainable.

Stack Overflow serves as a vital resource for programmers to resolve coding challenges, though not all queries succeed in finding answers. This study investigates such unsuccessful questions, analyzing question body length, accepted answer characteristics, external resource usage frequency and length, and question tags to identify patterns behind these failures. Findings reveal that questions tend toward shorter lengths and exhibit significantly more reliance on external resources compared to successful ones. Specifically, GitHub repositories are the most frequently shared resources; they are often repeated multiple times within a single question, whereas web links often occur as singular instances. Furthermore, questions struggling to find answers tend to reference more projects and rely more heavily on tagged technologies than those that succeed.

The wide variety of observed galaxy rotation curves suggests diverse inner density profiles for dark matter halos. Although often simplified as constant density isothermal cores, these profiles can be better understood through a polytropic model of dark matter self-gravity. By treating dark matter as a fluid where pressure depends on density via a polytropic equation of state, and allowing for either adiabatic (reversible) or irreversible thermodynamic processes, we generate preliminary density profiles. Our results demonstrate that assuming an adiabatic process yields a characteristic inner core structure, leading to considerable diversity among profiles that adequately explains the variety in rotation curves across different galaxies.

We introduce a novel framework for identifying individual climate values by analyzing their reading history of climate-related publications. Building upon this personalized value profile, we develop distinct interventions tailored to stimulate specific actions addressing climate change, thereby enhancing our capacity to combat environmental issues by precisely matching behaviors to users' unique motivations and addressing a previously overlooked gap in our research on understanding personal climate values and designing targeted behavioral interventions.

This study introduces an extensive and carefully annotated collection of 169,854 symptom extraction instances drawn from 10,804 patient reviews across 11 distinct languages to enable cross-lingual evaluation. Our benchmarks demonstrate that our proposed models outperform existing ones in extracussing symptoms for underrepresented language pairs, achieving top-tier results even when evaluating German data with English models or adapting French models to create tags. Additionally, we introduced two novel tasks: detecting sarcasm within reviews and identifying specific body parts mentioned. Sarcasm detection has practical value for analyzing low-star ratings, while body part identification supports task-specific applications like virtual tumor mapping. Finally, we explored the impact of domain shifts, observing that training models on electronic health records (EHR) and applying them to patient reviews yields superior performance compared to standard domain adaptation techniques.

The proposed method employs Recurrent Neural Networks to augment the capabilities of Partially Observable Markov Decision Process models, which are implemented using end-to-end Recurrent Neural Networks. By integrating memory modules based on state matrices, which offer theoretical advantages over Recurrent Lays and Partially Observable Markov Decision Process models, we integrate this method with attention mechanisms to highlight relevant features. Although spiking neural networks (SNNs) are recognized for their exceptional energy efficiency, a substantial amount of research is required to fully exploit this potential. A primary hurdle is the difficulty in training SNNs to match the accuracy of Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs). We introduce Reservoir Spiking Neural Networks (Reservoir SNNs), general-purpose classifiers that achieve performance comparable to standard ANNs while ensuring significantly reduced energy usage. This architecture functions by retaining membrane potentials of a reservoir of spiking neurons over extended durations. We evaluate this approach across image classification and speech recognition, demonstrating strong results that validate its effectiveness. Furthermore, we develop quantized variants of Reservoir SNNs that deliver attractive accuracy without the energy accuracy trade-off, enabling a direct comparison with unquantified models.

In this study, we examine the impact of strong magnetic fields on the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter. Our findings reveal that increased magnetic field intensity stiffens the equation of state, enabling higher maximum mass limits. Our next task is to explore the implications of these findings on neutron star radii and moment of inertia; subsequent research in our group will address this.

To address the urgent need for additional computing power in the race for Quantum supremacy, we introduce Pando, a system enabling collaborative computation across multiple user devices. Pando allows participants to jointly run classical simulations of the quantum circuits targeted for superclassical performance. Specifically, it maps circuit execution to multiple personal devices (PEDs), where each circuit bit is evaluated using a combination of classical and stochastic methods. With support for both iOS and Android personal devices, Pando triples output compared to a single device and improves resilience to noise by benchmarking superclassical circuits against lower-rate simulations.

This paper investigates how machine learning techniques, specifically neural networks, can be leveraged to accelerate the computation of eigenvalues for elliptic operators. We propose a novel adaptive sampling strategy tailored for approximation spaces derived from graph neural architectures, enabling the eigenvalues of elliptic operators to be estimated with significantly fewer samples than traditional finite element methods. Additionally, the study introduces an uncertainty quantification method based on quantifying loss function gradients to facilitate refinements in dense sampling regions. This data-driven methodology is demonstrated on eigenvalue problems involving complex boundary conditions.

We evaluate the Hausdorff dimensions of projection subspaces consisting of badly approximable numbers defined through intermediate $r$-adic $\beta$-expansions; these survivor sets correspond exactly to Combetta's previous work. Additionally, we demonstrate a striking finding where the dimension of a specific projection subspace reaches full unity. This subspace links $\mathbb{Z}_3$-adic $\beta$-expansion and exhibits a remarkably high degree of non-locally connected structure.

Building upon the recent developments in Deep Learning interpretations, this study explores the utility of DeepLICA—a recently proposed method for visualizing features and their contributions across samples and dimensions. This work introduces Privacy-Safe Federative Learning (PSFL), a privacy-secured framework addressing vulnerabilities in current secure techniques that predominantly focus on bandwidth conservation and expose gradient signals. Building upon our proposed method, we implement three distinct secure computational protocols, each supported by specific cryptosystems tailored for operations within this framework. Additionally, our approach introduces Secure Gradient Descent (SGD) to mitigate information leakage during training. Comprehensive evaluations using both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our methods. Furthermore, our experimental results indicate that PSFL achieves parity in convergence rate and model precision compared to standard federative learning.

This report details solution options designed for microcontroller-based driver validation, a device critical to a vehicle's motion control. Invalid driver operation can trigger severe microcontroller malfunction, potentially compromising vehicle control. Current methodologies for assessing drivers are confined to software-defined tests executed on a personal computer, lacking the capability to emulate crucial hardware-triggered events. This study introduces a hardware-in-the-loop approach that sim both software and hardware driver inputs, featuring four distinct test configurations implemented across two microcontrollers. Each setup utilizes dedicated input circuits, a reconfigurable state machine, and a test-specific peripheral circuit tailored to the specific microcontroller in use. All architectures are grounded on an FPGA-driven architecture. Testing execution relies on both computer-generated algorithms and autonomous, hardware-specific triggers. The individual circuitry for each of the four distinct test modes, along with specific implementations on two different controllers, are outlined.

Single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis faces significant statistical challenges due to high dimensionality and the scarcity of samples. To classify cell types in such settings, this study proposes a model class that projects data onto low-dimensional product space forms, specifically targeting the product of multivariate Gaussians. This framework yields two key insights: first, classification within these product space forms achieves at least a 10-fold performance boost compared to Euclidean spaces for scRNA-seq data; second, the mathematical structure of these projects naturally produces interpretable, discrete cell clusters. Notably, this approach determines cell cluster dimensions directly from limited sample sizes.

We investigate how orbital scattering of a stellar population influenced by a supermassive black hole (SMBH) is affected by close encounters. These encounters occur within an enclosed sphere of radius $R_e$, which is defined such that the enclosed stellar mass remains constant. This boundary radius is applied because, in clusters where stellar masses are much smaller than those of the black hole, most orbital energy is determined by the distance to this point where $R_e$ lies. We demonstrate that, for power-law mass functions, the scattering rate is modified by a specific power-law term derived from the mass function's slope. Additionally, we derived analytic expressions for the diffusion coefficient in velocity space, which depend on the mass function's power-law slope. When applying these results to a typical galactic nucleus, we find that scattering moves to lower orbital energies by approximately one to two orders of magnitude compared to the standard assumption of a uniform distribution of masses. Finally, we note that this effect is even more pronounced in elliptical galaxies, where scattering rates can be reduced by several orders of magnitude.

Stochastic Model Predictive Control (MPC) systems are implemented to address how system uncertainty influences plant behavior. This work focuses specifically on the optimization landscape optimization problem associated with stochastic MPC. The proposed method assumes that stochastic MPC utilizes quadratic cost functions together with linear system constraints, which are complemented by piecewise linear cost augmentations. By applying the subgradient method, an algorithm is devised to explicitly calculate gradients regarding the online optimization parameters within the framework of stochastic model predictive control. This approach allows for the implementation of gradient-based optimization techniques, capable of achieving faster convergence as well as requiring significantly reduced memory compared to standard stochastic MPC online solvers.

This study examines a specialized asymmetric noisy voter model involving two distinct species competing within a finite one-dimensional lattice. Unlike previous variations, this model incorporates direction-dependent noise: rightward transmission of the dominant species' identity is louder than the leftward one. We have constructed a rigorous dynamical framework to analyze the system's long-term behavior, identifying three distinct outcomes: total extinction of one species or neutral coexistence where both occupy equal lattice sites, and biased coexistence where one species dominates but the other maintains a fixed presence. This characterization holds across all noise levels and asymmetry degrees. Furthermore, by introducing additional perturbations such as biased voting tendencies, we explored multi-phase scenarios yielding more intricate distribution patterns. These physical interpretations are supported by both numerical data and rigorous mathematical theorems.

We demonstrate that the frustration-free ground states of local von Neumann algebras within infinite matrix product states on infinite lattices yield local algebras of type $II_{1}$ in all instances. Additionally, we posit that these algebras are essentially infinitely projective.

This research examines a photonic entanglement coherent feedback loop arrangement designed to regulate quantum correlations via thermal mechanisms. Our findings indicate that while entanglement remains fragile when thermal influence acts independently, it becomes robust via coherent feedback loops that protect it against thermal disturbances. Specifically, we demonstrate experimentally and through theory that matured entangled light generated by this system retains entanglement even after interacting with a weakly cooled heat bath for extended durations. Consequently, this apparatus offers a practical pathway for implementing quantum controllers based on feedback loops and explores potential applications in quantum information systems, including the construction of entanglement-induced and feedback-loop-based memory systems capable of functioning at or beyond fundamental thermal limits.

We compute and validate, via Monte Carlo methods, the integrated counterterms for a configuration involving two colliding particles and a tri-collinear triplet at the one-loop level within QCD. This study derives and validates a set of subtraction terms of order $\alpha_s^4$ required for differential distributions up to next-to-next-to-next-to-leading order (NNNLO) in QCD. Specifically, we calculate one-loop triple-collinear splitting operators for four distinct particle types—quarks, leptons, gluons, and photons—in the context of photon-initiated collisions.

This paper aims to prove Greenberg's strong theorem at one-dimensional local rings by utilizing an explicit equation defining the relevant elliptic curve, established by Silverman and Tate's criteria to determine rational points on $y^2=ax^2+b$. We will examine an algorithm developed explicitly to apply this strong approximation, and discuss examples demonstrating its utility.

Although sun dields are widespread throughout Indonesia, very few have been recorded, particularly those still functioning. We have developed an initiative named project Kompass to document these instruments by encouraging citizens to contribute by submitting images and data about local sundiles found in and around their neighborhoods. Supported by professional knowledge and technology, these community contributions facilitate the accurate recording and research of the instruments. Furthermore, we have created specialized software tools designed to manage the data provided by participants.

This study introduces Data and Energy Distribution using an Integrated Scheme (DED2IS) based on Time Slots (TS), which employs Time Slotting (TST) protocols to facilitate communication between vehicle-to-device nodes. A key innovation of DED2IS lies in its utilization of Time Slotting (TST) mechanisms within User Equipment (UE) systems, enabling the simultaneous exchange of data and power from source transmitters. This approach, referred to hereafter as DED2IS-TST, represents significant advancement in integrated communication and energy networks.

The surge in remote work mandates has accelerated the automation of experimental systems enabling remote verification. Recently, we demonstrated how this strategy applies to an optical cross-talk characterization experiment performed across geographically separated sites with the assistance of only chat-based communication. The current project extends that work into its automation phase, employing the Python library `moteflight` to steer equipment from one side and the `Jupyter` notebook ecosystem on the receiving end for data analysis and processing. The implementation has been generalized into a software framework suitable for replicating similar dual-location experiments, maintaining all connections over simple internet sockets. This software was distributed via `git` and can also function as a Jupyter kernel directly at one or both locations to support local execution needs.

Undirected bipartite graphs were previously utilized as a technical tool in restricted settings. Leveraging the benefits offered by this graph type, we are able to reassess an unsolved conjecture by Asser that pertains to the cl
ass of spectra. Specifically, we analyze how much the original constraints—imposing the use of undirected graphs and requiring bipartiteness—limit Asser's conjecture. Our investigation reveals two main outcomes: we provide a simplified undirected bipartite graph example that showcases the highest possible complexity for directed spectra, and we establish a strong connection between directed and undirected spectral problems. Consequently, this partial resolution yields a novel undirected bipartite spectrum with rigorous directed spectral complexity, and we demonstrate a rigorous connection between directed and undirected bipartite spectra. Finally, we show that there is an undirected bipartite graph that has a spectral complexity equal to that of a specific directed graph.

Electron probe size and current density are critical parameters that define the capabilities of a transmission electron microscope (TEM). While electrostatic phase plates have offered a path to enhancing contrast in conventional objective lenses, their integration as current-collecting components demands specific design attention to optimize contrast current and minimize probe dimensions. Using simulations, we examined design variables—including fill-factor, pixel configuration, and lens symmetry—and offered designs that offer improved current probe size metrics. These findings support the deployment of phase plate inserts within advanced single-foil TEM architectures aimed at further probe size reduction.

This article advances a comprehensive theory linking cognition across various physical substrates to neural spike patterns, utilizing information dynamics frameworks such as causal and informational difference theory. The model encompasses computational processes arising from various physical mechanisms—including symbolic computation, cellular automata, stochastic algorithms, and quantum computing—with the explicit goal of unifying theories of symbolic and statistical cognition. While quantum computing faces unique challenges requiring a specialized formulation of computational causal difference, it fits within the broader theory alongside other computing forms, converging with statistical cognition on a fundamental level.

We introduce a framework designed to train deep neural networks with guaranteed robustness against arbitrary worst-case perturbations up to a specified magnitude. This system employs an optimization-based approach that maximizes the accuracy of the trained model specifically against such worst-case threats. To execute this plan, a data-dependent, adaptive, yet computable certificate must be established for inversions within a designated robustness threshold; this certificate quantifies the model's confidence when encountering adversarial inputs. Leveraging recent theoretical advancements, we utilize a formal certificate to account for both limited data scenarios and computational constraints when addressing arbitrary worst-case perturbations. Consequently, the resulting deep learning frameworks demonstrate validated resistance against substantial noise injections, including the capability to withstand a Minkowski norm error of up to 1.0.

Rumor attenuation remains a critical challenge within social network research. This paper introduces a novel method designed to attain accurate predictions regarding rumor peak levels and attenuation coefficients, utilizing data from multiple sources. Hyperspectral image (HSI) pixel classification stands out as a critical task in HSI analysis, yet the scarcity of labeled samples and the massive feature dimensionality complicate extracting discriminative pixels from limited training data. This paper proposes a novel framework called Label Efficient Signal Dimensionality Reduction (LEDRED), designed to handle both pixels and neighboring contexts within HSI training sets without relying on labeled data. The core methodology involves reconstructing the class signal by aggregating and evaluating similar neighboring contexts. Specifically, we first map the spectrum of adjacent pixels to a lower-dimensional space using unsupervised dimensionality reduction techniques, such as those tested and evaluated. Next, we propose a novel class signal evaluator that leverages the mutual similarity spectrum between a target pixel and its neighbors. Finally, we determine the optimal reduced-dimensional space through a specific evaluation metric. The results demonstrate that the signal reconstructed from neighbors exhibits greater separability than the original HSI spectra. Furthermore, the LEDRED approach achieves superior classification accuracy compared to existing methods, especially when evaluating contexts under label-scarce conditions.

Quantum field theory formulations developed from Hamiltonians inherently uphold conservation and crossing symmetry, yet these properties are typically violated by perturbative Hamiltonian-derived amplitudes due to renormalization procedures. We propose a method to construct analytically continued, symmetry-respecting Green's functions by crossing-regularizing their perturbative expansions. This technique validates several recent findings: it confirms that parity-violating artifacts in polarized electron-positron annihilation cross-sections arise solely from renormalization-dependent symmetry breaking, it supports a class of analytically tractable QED vacuum structures that maintain these symmetries, and it yields a parquet-compatible QED variant derived via Hamiltonian constraints. Furthermore, we demonstrate that, in abelian QED and specific subranges relevant to experiments, the resulting continued amplitude matches standard computations; however, significant discrepancies emerge in higher energy regimes for multi-loop orders within quantum chromodynamics.

Gas-exposed monolayer TiSe$_2$ exhibits a complex interplay between excitonic condensation and a charge-density-wave (CDW) order. At low temperatures, this middle-gap state drives a metal-insulator transition; crucially, in charge-density-wave gaps associated with lattice distortions, such a dispersionless band cannot exist. Instead, we observe the coexistence of this midgap excitonic condensate with CDW ordering while transport measurements demonstrate unique critical scaling near the metal-insulator transition point that supports this dual order parameter model.

Current active learning algorithms often suffer from an uncritical adoption of the minimax entropy framework; these approaches to semi-supervised and semi-supervised active learning tasks fail to adequately consider entropy as a measure of uncertainty or sampling diversity. While these methods claim to optimize worst-case test error through probability distribution matching between labeled and unlabeled data using entropy constraints, they suffer from numerical instability during minimax optimization due to excessive scale sensitivity and instability, causing sample selection bias, thus degrading model performance. In response, we introduce Semi-Supervised Minimax-Entropy Active Learning (SE-MAX), an algorithm that rectifies these issues through three core innovations. Firstly, we incorporate two entropy-derived metrics that jointly reduce classification error while enhancing the representativeness of the labeled-unlabeled distribution pairs. Secondly, we apply gradient descent within Frank-Wolfe optimization, improving upon entropy-based approaches through a more stable, efficient search mechanism for the minimum cross-entropy. Thirdly, we leverage a minimax formulation to simultaneously optimize the labeling and unlabeled distributions to optimize the worst-case test error. Empirically, SE-MAX demonstrates robust performance, achieving approximately a 2% average accuracy increase over competing state-of-the-art baseline algorithms across multiple label-availability benchmarks.

Although prior studies have examined timbre similarity between song pairs using machine learning algorithms like Contrastive Learning and autoencoders to uncover relationships such as harmonic and timbral sequences, this research takes a distinct approach. By employing autoencoders, our work investigates timbre similarity within popular songs released every ten years from 1968 onward. We analyzed song timbres by extracting features from both audio data and chord progressions decimated to one chord per four bars, then calculated song-to-song similarity matrices using cosine distance on these reduced datasets. Our analysis reveals recurring diagonal patterns of similarity across decades and additional off-diagonal clusters indicating shared stylistic traits, such as acoustic guitar dominance in earlier years or synthesizers in more recent eras. We also observed that similarity tends to decrease with time distance, yet this trend is not consistent uniformly; for instance, the 1970s demonstrated a notably flatter distribution of similarity compared to subsequent periods.

Molecular motors, which are nanosized devices, are frequently evaluated in terms of the power they can generate. However, their operational dynamics are often described using coarse-grained models that focus on conformational transitions, paying little attention to conformational fluctuations. This oversight is problematic because such models fail to capture Brownian fluctuations, which result from thermal noise, as well as the specific influence mechanisms they lack on motor function. We demonstrate that these currents can generate an active force that significantly impacts the system's behavior. This study introduces a model where ISPs negotiate and share revenues to align their investment efforts through collaboration. We first demonstrate that among homogeneous ISPs, cooperation strictly increases investment and total content provider utility compared to non-cooperative scenarios. We then examine heterogeneity, finding that while cooperation still yields higher system-wide benefits, it may result in unequal investment levels and reduced payoffs for smaller ISPs relative to non-cooperative strategies. Finally, we define and maximize welfare by determining optimal utility distribution among ISPs, noting that sophisticated, asymmetric ISPs may strategically opt for non-cooperation to secure higher individual benefits.

This brief note demonstrates that any two compositions formed by adjoining functors with property X exhibit weak naturality, where X can be any of the following: functoriality, ultrametricity, universality, or universality in the context of categorical objects and morphisms. Additionally, the authors show that exhibiting weak naturality constitutes precisely the weakest condition required to reconstruct the full concept of functoriality.

We examine how $𝛼$-attractor models, encompassing both exponential and polynomial forms within $𝛼$-canonical frameworks with power-law mixing, align with cosmological datasets. Fitting these general inflationary potentials to data highlights the distinctiveness of our proposed exponential and polynomial models, demonstrating superior performance over $𝛼$-attractors derived from linear symmetries. Furthermore, by utilizing linearly approximated symmetries derived from grand unified theories to constrain these potentials, our results support an alignment between $𝛼$-attractor inflationary models and GUT-scale physics.

We present 'Cross,' a novel distribution for modeling the time series of monthly asset returns that integrates 'Cross', the cross-sectional returns distribution as a fundamental component. By linking the moments (up to the fourth order) of this cross-sectional distribution with the moments of aggregate returns, we establish a duality between the two distributions. Specifically, we treat the means, standard deviations, skewness, and kurtosis derived from the cross-sectional returns as meaningful return characteristics. Within our 'Cross' framework, we utilize Assumption A to model the joint distribution of means and standard deviations across assets, further assuming moment invariance in both the series lengths of returns and the cross-sectional aggregation. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of our model in asset allocation and portfolio construction by implementing a simulation study.

By implementing a variational autoencoder, our methodology effectively segregates artifacts from vital signal components. These reconstructed symptoms subsequently undergo either direct classification or classification after aggregating relevant features. We present an ab initia calculation of the long-range electric dipole transition amplitudes for $1s2s\ ^3$S $\rightarrow\ ^1$S and $1s2s\ ^1$S $\rightarrow\ ^1$S electronic transitions within tritium ($^3$H) using modern many-body physics techniques. The energy-dependent dipole amplitude, $D_{fi}(\omega)$, is decomposed into distinct components: a "Main" part, representing the $|\rm 1s\rangle\langle2s\rangle$ matrix element computed with initial and final states isolated; a "Core" part, accounting for all two-electron excitations excluding those to the $2s$ orbital; and a "Tail" part, capturing all two-electron excitations to orbitals other than $2s$. In this study, the "Core" and "Tail" terms are evaluated using the Quantum Monte Carlo method with fixed-node approximation, while the "Main" term is calculated using the M$\acute{\text{o}}$ller-Plesset perturbation theory up to the fourth order, combined with a variational Coupled Cluster single-and-double excitation approach, plus its second-order correction. Employing the "Tail" term expressed as perturbation theory on a Tail basis, the total amplitude $D_{fi}(\omega)$ is reconstructed, enabling the computation of the transition probability and the corresponding electric dipole transition rate

We offer an accessible introduction to equivariant cohomology under the action of a finite group, defining it via the twist category derived from group actions on a tensor category, specifically utilizing the tensor-trivial category as the foundation. Using categorical tools, we establish linking equivariant cohomology closely with twisted cohomology. We then generalize the Munn-Zimmermann Theorem within this categorical framework. Furthermore, we clarify how twisting categories with periodic inversions corresponds to gauge theories on tori and determine the twists within this specific setting.

This paper examines strategies to improve the environment within an academic department, arguing that improvements in communal bonds and collaborative efforts effectively mitigate negative dynamics. Additionally, we explore how targeted, discrete, and low-cost interventions can trigger widespread, self-reinforcing positive shifts, fostering transformative changes throughout the department's culture. Drawing on established principles of resilience and nonlinear dynamics—specifically within adaptive systems and chaos theory, such as the蝴蝶 effect (butterfly effect)—we explore innovative, adaptable approaches to address both immediate and enduring challenges faced by faculty and departments in evolving times. By fostering stronger collaborations and leveraging these dynamic principles, departments can effectively neutralize negative dynamics and ignite self-sustaining waves of success.

This study establishes the boundedness criteria for the fractional series operator $T_\alpha$ acting as $L^p(\mathbb{T}) \to L^q(\mathtt{t})$. It demonstrates that $T_\alpha$ is not bounded whenever $\frac{1}{p} - \frac{1}{q} \geq \alpha - N$. Additionally, it presents explicit explicit formulas for the Fourier coefficients of $T_\alpha$ and extends these results to establish similar boundedness conditions and formulas for the fractional transform defined on $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ to $L^q(\mathtt{t})$.

This paper presents an experimental evaluation of seller strategies within non-fully-credible second-price sealed-bid auctions featuring a single, privately valued item and risk-neutral participants. Evidence indicates sellers often deviate from first-principles guidelines, failing to maximize apparent revenue by underestimating competitor bids, accepting lower prices, or manipulating information through item attributes, thereby compromising auction integrity.

This study investigates how anisotropic perturbations in the cosmological background evolve within an $f(R)$ universe model designed to explain dark energy. We demonstrate that, regardless of anisotropic conditions during the radiation or matter eras, the background tends toward isotropy. Furthermore, since our model predicts a transition from an anisotropic state in the very early universe to one of near-perfect isotropy later on, anisotropic effects become negligible. Consequently, the model's predictions for cosmological parameters remain robust.

We investigate the Gr\"obner bases within this context, analyzing the conditions that result in distinct polynomial orders of separation for intersecting Hessenberg types. Furthermore, our work extends certain theoretical findings from previous studies of partial flag varieties into more generalized settings, applying these insights particularly prominent in Hessenberg varieties where local defining ideals can now describe the polynomial functions governing the local topology of the variety. The analysis deepens understanding regarding how Gr\"obner bases reflect the geometric constraints imposed by the Borel subgroup invariance and grading structures inherent to these objects.

While Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are a premier tool for AI-generated imagery, their application within fine art remains underappreciated. This paper introduces a method for employing GANs to create AI-assisted fine art painting by modeling brushstrokes as low-poly 2D plans within image space. Using a 2D-2D translation GAN, the system learns a mapping from a simple latent code—which directly corresponds to a non-polymorphic brushstroke layout—to a real-space representation that includes color and tonal variation. The research demonstrates this approach through hands-on interactions with AI to compose and modify digital sketches. The output AI artworks are available for examination at: https://www.goodlabs.com/ai-paint.

We introduce Dasp, novel approach for question-asking from texts. Our technique utilizes additional knowledge beyond provided context and established data sets like, Quiz Bowl to improve performance. Our approach includes four distinct phases: phase-1 involves text mining to extract candidates for potential inquiries; phase-2 synthesizes facts across various documents for factual verification; phase-3 utilizes a Natural Language Processing model for precise question formulation; final phase involves generating appropriate queries for a human respondent. Our approach was named DASPER due its ability achieve state art results using only 20 percent training data compared to existing systems. Our system scored in top 5 positions overall during competition, achieving number one ranking for textual analysis tasks. Our methodology was developed specifically to address challenges presented by real world text-based quizzes featuring multi document source material. We created comprehensive dataset consisting recordings from competitions featuring approximately 5,000 questions derived from six seasons worth text sources containing over million words. We also proposed novel evaluation metrics focused detecting hallucinations identifying redundant information among answers providing more granulated assessment capabilities.

This work examines the evolution of both differential rotation and magnetization profiles across various shock transitions. We observe that while failed explosions do not necessarily induce fast instabilities in the post-shock region, successful supernovae frequently do so, significantly influencing how the stellar core evolves post-explosion. Consequently, progenitor models exhibiting steeper or more pronounced dips in density and specific heat ratio ($\gamma$) consistently yield more violent post-shock conditions. Furthermore, when the pre-shock angular velocity is sufficiently high, the post-shock region invariably develops both rotation and magnetization, creating favorable environments for rapid core collapse. Although the successful supernova scenario often triggers fast instabilities in the immediate aftermath, viscous diffusion soon erodes the resulting density gradient, suppressing the threat of a catastrophic stellar disruption.

Although the Deep Learning-based classification of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) has gained significant traction, prior studies often suffer from overfitting and excessive computational costs, as they are typically trained using entire functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) frames. These issues result in over-optimistic accuracy reports and inefficient training processes. To address these challenges, this study employs data augmentation techniques, including total reversal, left-right flipping, and intensity normalization, alongside the selection of regions within the space-time volume identified as critical for distinguishing between ADHD and control groups. Specifically, we utilized a temporal mask to isolate the most informative slices and a three-dimensional attention mechanism to pinpoint the most relevant x, y-z spatial coordinates. To evaluate the efficacy of this approach, we retrained three architectures—Residual Networks (ResNet), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), and Hybrid ResLSTM—using only these critical areas of interest. Using the ADIDA dataset, our results demonstrate that Modified ResNet achieves an exceptional diagnostic accuracy of 70.46% while training on approximately 95.2% less data volume compared to standard approaches, thereby confirming that focusing on essential features from fMRI data yields both highly accurate classifications and improved efficiency.

This work examines heat rectification within quantum Hall systems that exhibit longitudinal dissipation. We identify two mechanisms for achieving thermal rectification: one based on varying sample width and another on sample length. We also analyze the influence of a longitudinal dissipation channel on rectification performance, suggesting that coupling with a one-dimensional dissipation channel offers a promising approach for thermal diode functionality. Rectification efficacy is maximized when quantum Hall samples are coupled to normal metal leads. Additionally, we observe that coupling two dissipation channels in a series configuration acts more effectively than doing so in parallel. Finally, we confirm that connecting quantum Hall regions serially with a single defect is a potent strategy for achieving robust thermal rectification.

This paper introduces LiD2, an advanced data storage on DNA framework. The proposed storage architecture achieves a 2× improvement in asymptotic data rates compared to conventional methods. Furthermore, it integrates storage and retrieval operations via a single PCR primer pair per partition, thereby reducing amplification by half. By implementing a data correction protocol based on distance metrics, data integrity can be recovered even in the event of permanent loss. Additionally, the proposed approach enables the critical capability of in-place data reorganization within stored partitions. Ultimately, computational and material efficiencies are maximized throughout the entire lifecycle. To demonstrate this, we present the mathematical proof for the proposed storage architecture and provide computer experiments validating the proposed correction protocols.

"This work examines how a single oscillator interacting with others creates waves across various landscapes. By examining ridges in three dimensions and valleys in two dimensions, we observe that the medium directly impacts wave propagation. Key factors include the medium's resistance and how deeply an oscillator sinks into depressions. These variables control speed in both two and three dimensions, demonstrating clear links between wave motion and physical topography."

This paper introduces two novel algorithms for estimating entropy that are free from assumptions regarding the underlying distribution, focusing instead on samples drawn from it. First, we detail an interactive protocol involving two parties holding shared samples, who jointly estimate entropy. Second, we present a non-interactive application of this method for an individual party to estimate the entropy using their own data. Our proofs of correctness rely on information-theoretic security. Notably, these methods are efficient when the input data's entropy is bounded away from zero, a condition necessary for validity. For the interactive scenario, we achieve both communication complexity of $\tilde O(\sqrt{H/n})$ and computational cost of $\tilde O(\sqrt{H}/n)$ per participant; for the non-interactive case, the runtime scales as $\tilde O(\sqrt{H}/n)$. Here, $H$ represents the sample-entropy, defined as the entropy of the source given $n$ observed samples.

Imaging biobanks are accumulating vast collections of paired medical images and clinical annotations, representing a significant resource for advancing artificial intelligence in healthcare. As these collections expand, they raise critical questions regarding data architecture, storage systems, implementation strategies, and standards. This paper outlines the conceptual design, essential standards, and practical guidelines for imaging biobanks. We examine current implementations to extract lessons relevant to the development of new ones, covering metadata modeling, secure storage solutions, and policy governance. Furthermore, we address the construction of reference benchmarks, including a proposed unified dataset of clinical labels derived from varied healthcare records, alongside a toolset of refutative benchmarks to mitigate research myopia. Leveraging these initiatives, we aim to shape the future trajectory of research biobank methodology and resource development.

This research examines the role of data augmentation in predicting pathology slides using deep learning. Our approach treats this task as a classification problem limited by small datasets of clinical feature annotations and corresponding slide images, leveraging augmentation to enhance model performance. The paper analyzes two scenarios: first, predicting diagnoses from clinical features alone with assistance from histology images; and second, predicting pathology slides based on diagnosis labels and clinical features. Performance is evaluated using classification accuracy over 100 folded cross-validation, comparing original models against augmented data variants. Results indicate that without clinical features, simple data augmentation outperforms complex strategies like GANs and BERT; however, when clinical features are available, simple and complex augmentations yield comparable classification accuracy. The study concludes that simple data augmentation remains highly effective for integrating information across pathology slides and clinical features to boost deep learning efficacy.

Polymatroidal ideals are highly structured commutative monomial ideals that serve as a broad and natural generalization of matroid ideals. While their theoretical properties have been examined in multiple studies, the explicit decomposition of these ideals into prime ideals and the determination of the specific prime decompositions that eliminate all polynomials greater than a certain degree have received little attention until recently. This work revisits these foundational aspects, offering specific characterizations of polymatroidal ideals through both prime decomposition and minimal generating sets by excluding those generated in high degrees. Furthermore, we provide novel insights into polymatroidal ideals defined on graphs by supplying a complete characterization of graph-based ideals that possess minimal generators consisting solely of edges.

We utilize the Data Quality Flag (DQF) from the Kepler mission to detect planetary events, a methodology that proves effective even for low-contrast signals difficult to identify through traditional light curves. This new approach allows us to statistically analyze the resulting planet mass-ratio function, demonstrating consistency with findings from the Kepler dataset which has been confirmed via Keypoint Explorer analysis.

We introduce a technique for computing shadows in environments with complex, non-triangular geometry based on rays that conform to light transport. This approach overcomes limitations associated with standard ray tracing by eliminating the requirement for a triangular mesh, thereby offering greater geometric flexibility. Additionally, it avoids the need to calculate intersections along rays, which enhances rendering efficiency. Despite these advantages, the method preserves high accuracy by accurately accounting for geometric occlusion and shadows produced by how light travels through an scene.

This study introduces an enhanced methodology for the probabilistic estimation of Origin-Destination (O-D) demand utilizing regularization techniques to refine covariance matrix estimation for the Large Neighbors Lasso (LaN) algorithm. Previously, this methodology depended upon Lasso, which proved insufficient when accounting for the regulatory effects of neighboring cells. Results demonstrate that applying LaN significantly accelerates convergence and generates superior covariance matrix approximations compared to Lasso. Furthermore, this study introduces a formulation for incorporating the variance associated with O-D estimates. Ultimately, findings confirm that regulatory neighbors Lasso demands does not only improve speed but also resilience to the variance of origin-destination pairs, particularly in scenarios where origin-destination estimates are subject to variance.

This study analyzes the stability dynamics of phase-locked regimes within a ring composed of three oscillators featuring nonlinear Coulomb coupling and weak nonlinear frequency dispersion deemed negligible in the clustered phase. Notably, the presence of dispersion fundamentally alters asymptotic stability. Specifically, a cluster configuration stabilized by pure Coulomb coupling becomes unstable when dispersion is introduced; conversely, clusters initially unstable under Coulomb rules may gain stability with the inclusion of dispersion. Furthermore, the integrated approach employing averaged equations of motion facilitated by canonical transformations demonstrates that a Hopf bifurcation arises through phase locking as system parameters shift. Additionally findings indicate a potential alignment between the Hopf emergence and a Hopf phenomenon predicted by a reduced ordern model.

Lov\'{a}s and Wilson introduced two algorithms that generate uniform spanning trees in $O(m \log n + n^\alpha)$ expected time for $\alpha > 1$, where $m$ and $n$ represent the number of edges and vertices, respectively. In this study, we introduce a hybrid hybrid method combining their approaches using an optimized cutoff point. This proposal achieves $O((m + n^\alpha)\log n)$ expected time complexity, offering greater efficiency than the original implementation. Furthermore, we present a theoretical analysis of our algorithm's performance across various inputs and construct sizes, supported by numerical experiments that verify our findings.

This study utilizes the optimal control method to analyze control coil placement requirements that achieve a specific quasi-symmetric magnetic configuration featuring nested flux surfaces. The model employs a simplified, high-optimization scenario with only four control coils, highlighting the sensitivity of optimal positions to system parameters such as the desired quasi-symmetry metric and magnetic configuration geometry. Findings indicate that positioning requirements are highly sensitive to these variables; furthermore, enhancing the flexibility of the magnetic configuration's shape generally expands the necessary physical scale, particularly for the poloidal dimensions. Without further coils, higher-order symmetry metrics cannot be optimized independently of configuration shape, causing significant shifts in coil placement. Introducing a fifth coil allows for simultaneous maximization of shape flexibility and symmetry. The research concludes by proposing potential control strategies for the QUICS project based on these findings.

We introduce a planar waveguide configuration for a single-mode continuous-flow microchannel thermometry application. Resonant proton NMR signals serve as an effective method for assessing temperature gradients across planar cut surfaces of the water-filled microchannel. Resonant frequency shifts of protons correlated with temperature changes allow for thermometry, while echo-intensity reductions, driven by longitudinal and transverse relaxation mechanisms, provide gradient mapping. The experimental setup involved injecting deuterated water into planar reactor components at various locations and monitoring NMR signals using a high-resolution spectrometer. Using 2-D MATLAB algorithms, we calculated resonant frequencies and echo-intensity profiles, which were subsequently validated through numerical simulations. The resulting experimental data for both temperature gradients and proton NMR intensity align closely with the predicted simulation values.

Utilizing Tully-McCurdy theory, we examine Bose-Einstein condensation mixtures containing two species of unequal mass. Our analysis reveals that while the system's phase space features allow for up to two distinct condensates, the thermodynamic equilibrium state supports only one. Consequently, the number of achievable condensates is limited to half the total distinct species ($N/2$), rather than matching the total species count $N$. This prediction holds for systems with $N=2$ and extends to larger mixtures up to ten or more components. We attribute this phenomenon to the specific requirements for thermal equilibrium within multi-component systems, which restrict possible ground states despite theoretical phase availability, a mechanism applicable beyond these specific mixtures to similar physical systems. This prediction can be tested experimentally by comparing observed transitions to those predicted by standard many-body frameworks like Quantum Monte Carlo simulations or many-Body Localization theories.

Sunspots are known to generate magnetically powerful transient events linked to flares and/or flares. Previous studies of similar phenomena in other star systems have yielded mixed results, with some detecting them and others not. Observing one such event around AD Leo provides an opportunity to investigate whether these phenomena occur outside of our solar system. Using GREGOR 1.5m telescope data from a multi-wavelength observation campaign on 16 October, 2022, we tracked the magnetic transients induced by a significant flare detected in Leo AD. Our observations reveal one such feature, classified as Type-II, moving across a sunspot at speeds between 100-250 km/s. Additionally, our analysis of the obtained spectra indicates that this feature emits as a reconnection jet associated with the flare activity.

We present a proof of the Madsen-Weiss theorem derived from the principle of madness, which demonstrates that the homotopy type of the space of framed immersions of spheres into high-dimensional Euclidean spaces is controlled by the homotopy type of the space of framed maps. Our argument relies on the stability theorem of b-principle established by Hirsch. Specifically, we construct an explicit formula for the framed immersions of spheres into high-dimensional Euclidean spaces using configuration space integrals, which are then applied to the b-principle to show that any such framed immersion which is homotopically equivalent to a framed map. By applying the b-principle again, we obtain a strong version of the b-Hirsch theorem. As a corollary, we obtain the strong b-Hirsch theorem.

This paper investigates a scaling assessment of the Balancing Domain Decompositions by Constraints (BDDc) preconditioner applied to second-order elliptic problems with elliptic interfaces. Addressing an elliptic variational form with mixed boundary conditions, we employ the flexible local orthogonal projection multilevel Schur complement method (FLOPMSB), implemented within the ALMA library. ALMA offers enhanced ALGB-based implementations of this preconditioner.

The BDDc framework utilizes finite element partitions with overlapping interfaces. We examine the spectral behavior of our ALBCMB preconditioner by analyzing its underlying flow and specific choices of local solvers and proximal balancing techniques. Furthermore, to understand the impact of our neighboring constraints on algorithm stability, we examine equilibrium conditions derived from flow analysis and BDDc-specific balance analysis.

Tags have emerged as a prominent mechanism for users to organize and retrieve information across diverse platforms such as social networks, forums, and wikis. As tagging employs an open architecture allowing users to create arbitrary tags without administrative oversight, undesirable content like offensive labels can occasionally appear. Consequently, closed architectures employing pre-vetted, administrative terms are increasingly favored to replace openness. This study investigates user tagging patterns within open systems by analyzing Wikipedia contributions by banned editors. We demonstrate that individuals banned from the platform frequently utilize inappropriate tags, offering empirical support for our finding. This suggests such platforms benefit from prohibiting individual users from autonomously defining tags, which is crucial to preserving a high-quality tag ecosystem. The study extends prior work by providing nuanced findings based on subject domains and demonstrates that inappropriate tag usage by recipients varies significantly based on the specific domain of the tag, implying tailored moderation might be more effective than blanket supervision. The authors also propose employing supervised machine learning to pinpoint and remove problematic tags automatically.

This study examines the incompressible FENE dumbbell model when low-frequency effects are present. By leveraging an estimated bound on the low-frequency component, we establish bounds for both the sum and difference solutions of two distinct problems, handling both scenarios with and without a fixed initial difference. Our approach extends and enhances a recent result by Li and Li. We handle more comprehensive Besov space frameworks and generalize their methods by incorporating additional spaces such as $H^m_{1}$ and $H^m_{1}_{1}$. Mobile Integrated Access and Backhaul (mIAB) gNodeBs enhance connectivity for user equipment (UE) by aggregating the resources from multiple gNodeBs into a single mobile backhaul link. This capability is especially beneficial for clusters of UEs with high data demands. However, existing mIAB solutions fail to provide optimal resource allocation when multiple such groups share the network simultaneously. To address this deficiency, this paper introduces a novel cross-group multi-objective optimization framework. Our approach jointly optimizes transmission power and bandwidth allocation to simultaneously enhance sum throughput and spectral efficiency. To achieve this, the study applies the Sequential Linear Programming (SLP) algorithm, facilitating a global optimum-derived distribution of resources. Extensive simulations confirm that our proposed scheme significantly outperforms current alternatives by more than 30% in system sum throughput and spectral efficiency.

This study investigates the interconnections among hyperparameters for a specific algorithm and evaluates their impact on performance stability. Through experimental analysis using two optimization algorithms—Nelder-Mead (N-M) and Coordinate Descent (CD)—applied to a synthetic function across ten-dimensional space, we demonstrate significant non-linear interactions between parameters and their distinct effects on optimization outcomes. Findings indicate that only half specific pairings involve meaningful interactions for the N-M method, with the Hooke-Thomas (HH) combination showing the strongest relationships. Conversely, the CD algorithm exhibits interactions among all parameter pairs. Ultimately, we argue that hyperparameter tuning should not occur in isolation; instead, considering combined configurations and their interactions leads to more stable algorithm performance.

We introduce a novel curriculum for training and assessing RL agents that features controlled dynamics designed to test generalization across sequential tasks. This framework simulates an academic setting where students learn within a guided syllabus, creating environments that span from chaotic to structured curricula with varying degrees of support. This flexible approach enables researchers to unlock curriculum-induced generalization potentials or isolate curriculum effects by enabling comparisons against random environments and other structures. We also propose methodologies for tracing learned skills through sequences of tasks to enable finer-grained generalization tests. Initially, this framework applies to both discrete and continuous environments, supporting models ranging from simple policies to more complex systems like world models and meta-learners.

Liger is an open-source Python framework designed for large-scale, data-intensive statistical analyses on Apache Spark, with an emphasis on reusing existing data transformations and statistical tests across applications. As data volumes continue to expand, applying distributed data analytics to terabyte and petabyte scales becomes increasingly demanding; therefore, Liger aims to simplify this process by enabling data scientists to concentrate on their statistical inquiries while adhering to reproducible research principles. Liger incorporates multiple technologies, including modules for data reduction, test execution, and merging results. The Data Reduction System (DRS), a highlight of Liger, performs sampling and transformation of terabyte datasets down to manageable sizes suitable for specific tests, while preserving original data references to facilitate final aggregation. While other systems, such as Dr. Reduce, offer sampling capabilities, Liger distinguishes itself through capabilities for both wide and deep transformations and customized samples. The user interface supports various formats, such as Parquet and Avro, through its data readers and writers, and it reads metadata using MetaStore. The DRS leverages Spark's data sampling and transformations, while its test generation modules employ data-driven and modeling approaches to filter reduced datasets. Finally, the DRS accurately reconstructs input data statistics by featuring sophisticated reconstruction algorithms. The DRS utilizes wide transformations, exemplified by Liger's test modules, alongside the delta-chi module for customized and deep transformations, while the Liger merge and merge-all modules are utilized to merge results.

Integrating data from multiple sources holds great promise for achieving a comprehensive understanding of the environment. However, most existing fusion techniques—such as hierarchical, early, and intermediate approaches—often overlook the distinct physical characteristics of individual sensing modalities. To address this gap, we introduce a novel hierarchical fusion framework. Unlike its counterparts, this method ferves information directly from the raw hierarchy into final understanding, preserving semantic specifics across all transformation stages to facilitate physical characteristic retention. To demonstrate, we develop a multi-modal 3D object detection system utilizing deep fusion techniques. This system integrates instances segmentation and object recognition modules, fusing output from three distinct levels: anchor boxes, 3D parameters, and final object instances. Evaluations on the Oxford Robot Vision dataset confirm that this hierarchical approach surpasses early and intermediate fusion strategies, yielding superior detection performance.

This research introduces a decision-specific analysis framework designed to study features related to ICU admission during COVID-19 infections. By zeroing in on these targeted variables, we facilitate better ICU resource allocation, thereby supporting more effective management practices and streamlined scheduling. A key advantage of concentrating on these particular traits over comprehensive patient data is a dramatic decrease in both computational complexity and temporal requirements. Furthermore, by pinpointing specific risk factors, clinicians can refine their management strategies. Leveraging metrics such as correlation, feature importance from gradient boosting, and mutual information, we identified six critical indicators: current ICU occupancy, patient age, partial pressure of oxygen in arterial blood, duration of respiratory failure, time elapsed since symptom onset, and serum creatinine levels. Findings from this analysis are expected to yield beneficial insights for healthcare professionals.
